Whether it be tropical or cold countries, some species of vultures are sure to be found. Vultures of tropical countries are mostly of the Indian variety. They build their nests on the upper part of tall trees, primarily of banyan trees. While other birds build their nests with bits of dry grass and straw, vultures never do so. Their nests are somewhat open; however, for the protection of the eggs, straw is added. They lay their eggs in sparse quantity. The eggs are a light blue colour, quite large in size. The mother vulture cannot properly hatch her eggs. Instead, they break open with the heat of the sunlight. When vultures go to a distant dung-heap, during their absence salamanders come and eat up the eggs. Some say that due to eating too many of these eggs, the salamanders or iguanas often die. The body of the vulture bristles with different kinds of worms. These worms are found even in their nests.

Among birds, vultures are very sharp-sighted. Their beaks are extremely hard and can even pierce stones. The strength of their beaks is very close to that of a bird called banrui. They eat the flesh of animals by slicing them neatly with their beaks. Even when eating rotten flesh, they do not get food poisoning. Vultures are natureʼs self-created scavengers. In Bengali it is said, “On land the vulture, in water, the shark”. In Sanskrit the verb shak means “do”. The sentence “He can do it” is sah shaknoti in Sanskrit. With the suffix ktin we obtain the word shakti. In translating the word “battery” we have the verb shak, and adding lyut́ to it, we have the word shakan. With the verb shak and with the suffix uń we derive the word shaktu, meaning fried gram-powder, which gives strength when eaten. Shaktu > shattu > shátu > chátu. From the verb shak we derive the name of the bird shakunta. ( 5 )

We have said that although the shakun (vulture) is carnivorous, it does not eat the flesh of living animals. When an animal lies in the dung-heap, so long there is any life in it, the vulture never comes to eat its flesh. In this regard, the vulture is superior to human beings. Humans kill living animals to eat their flesh, while the vulture never eats the flesh of living animals. It only eats the flesh of dead animals, which are its natural food. Human beings think that vultures are cruel creatures; they think that tigers are monsters and are very cruel. Yet even the tigress – the legendary she-monster – has endless affection for her baby:
Bághini rudhir páne nirata lolupá
Ápan santáne táro agádh mamatá.
Parasútaghátinii putaná gopiirúpá
Nija putre stanya dáne kareni khalatá.
Bághinii rákśasii baŕa nirday jagate
Tárá kintu shataguńe bhálo ámáhate.
–Jadugopal Chattopadhyay

[The tigress is always tempted to drink blood, Yet for her own babies she has boundless affection. Putaná as milkmaid murders the children of others, Yet never failed in her duty to nurse her own babe. The tigress, the she-monster, so cruel in this world, Yet they are hundred times better than ourselves.]

Even the vulture has tremendous affection for its own child. This bird appears cruel but is highly devoted in her maternal love, and is said to have carefully nurtured and nourished the deserted daughter of a celestial nymph until the sage Kanva took her to his hermitage. Since the bird shakunta nurtured the baby, the sage Kanva named the baby girl shakuntalá or “the girl nurtured by shakunta”. Yes, all these terms are for the Indian vulture or Vulture indica. In the country of utmost cold, covered with snow on top of the Alps, some vultures also live. The best vultures species in the world live on top of the Alps.

[As told earlier] eagles, like vultures, cannot build compact nests with bits of dry grass and straw. On the Alpine mountains they gather pieces of stone and press them together to build something similar to a house in which they have their nest. Yes, the eagle is part of the larger family of vultures. Yet some eagles species are much larger in size than the species of Indian vultures or Vulture Indica. Monkey-eating eagles or sheep-snatching eagles are much larger in size than Indian vultures. Eagles of the Pacific Ocean region swoop down upon monkeys, lift them up and eat them. Alpine eagles swoop down upon the lambs of their choice in a herd of sheep and lift them up. They even swoop down and carry away big sheep. The condor species of Alpine eagle residing in the Alps are the largest among flying birds. Individually some of them look like large men. They fly at a terrific speed. They also cannot build their nests; they live in eyrie. Yet whether it is the eagle, condor or Indian vulture, each has a very hard beak. The vulture, of course, is looked upon as an ominous bird. The god Saturn whom people want to keep away from out of fear and to worship outside their house, touching their hands to their heads, taking prasád [sacred offerings] of the god but never carrying them home ( 6 ) – according to some Puranas, the vulture is the mount of that god Saturn. ( 7 )

Kite: River-gull, seagull and white-breasted kite: Kites (cil) are everywhere in the world except in predominantly cold countries. Indian kites are usually subdivided into three different species: the ordinary or black kites (krśńa cil), white kites, and river gulls or seagulls. Gradually kites are diminishing in number. Seagulls (gáuṋg cil) build their nests in big trees adjoining ocean beaches. Even their number is decreasing. White kites (shauṋkha cil) are barely visible. In our childhood we used to see two to four white kites every day. We used to see the nilkant́ha or blue-throated bird, phiuṋe [fork-tailed bird], and doel [magpie robin of Bengal] (it is a small bird, yet extremely carnivorous; not as cruel as hawks, and having a pleasant voice). Yet in later times, for mysterious reasons the blue-throated bird, fork-tailed bird and magpie robin of Bengal were all lost to an unknown world. I surmise that since the air of the adjoining city became polluted, and due to the absence of ozone in the air, they are disappearing rapidly. I hardly come across white kites, that is, shauṋkha cils; yet in the art of swooping down to earth from on high to carry away their prey, they surpass the black kites and seagulls. In the Jhumur songs of Ráŕh it is mentioned:
Shauṋkhaciler mato humŕye paŕye go,
Se keŕye liye khetye cáy lo!
[Swooping down like white kites He wants to eat by snatching away.]

Black kites are becoming extinct due to shortage of food. Seagulls are decreasing in number due to water pollution. Water pollution is prevalent all over the world. Due to polluted water from mills and factories, the water of rivers and oceans has become polluted, causing fish to die in endless numbers. Since fish and frogs are dying in such large numbers, for this very reason seagulls are nearly extinct. Hence water pollution is responsible for the extinction of seagulls.

Similarly, due to the polluted water that flows into the Mediterranean from European countries, its water has been rendered poisonous, and its marine life is about to become extinct. The flying fish and flying frog have disappeared behind the black curtain of history. That is why the seagulls of the Mediterranean coastal areas are becoming extinct. During my stay in Spain in Valencia, I used to sit on a hillock near the Mediterranean coast. Yet I never came across a single seagull. I enquired of the local people and gathered that since the fish are becoming scarce, the seagulls are also becoming extinct.

In Bengal, especially East Bengal, which was earlier famous for its ample supply of fish, the fish have now become scarce and costly. The shrimp, mango fish, hilsa, and flat fish (bhet́ki) are not only scarce, even the semi-marine fish that live in sweet as well as saline water are also rapidly decreasing in number. By eating them, the seagulls manage to survive. Thus they are also advancing towards extinction. Human beings do not eat white kites. Then why are they becoming extinct? This should be investigated. ( 8 )

Crane: In the whole world there were about twenty six different species of cranes (sárasa). Of these, seven species reside in India. By the word kośacaiṋcu we mean the seven types of cranes, and not other species. Today the crane is looked upon as an ancient bird of India. It is surmised that in the remote past this bird came to India from central eastern Asia, from the outer Mongolian region. Compared to the inclement climate of outer Mongolia, they preferred to remain in the more congenial environment of India. Indian cranes today are wholly Indian, and even with the changes of season they never stir outside India and migrate to other regions as do the shyámá bird [a song bird of the thrush family], blue-throated bird and cátaka [rainy season bird]. Although the crane is a completely carnivorous bird, it is not lacking in tenderness. Yet people never try to domesticate them as pets. Probably in a domesticated environment, they might not be able to adjust and would die prematurely. Once in India there were plenty of brown-coloured cranes. Nowadays, one does not see enough of these birds. Just like white kites, they are either on the way to extinction or are wholly extinct. ( 9 )

The second meaning of karat́a is “crane”. This long-billed crane is found in nearly every place in the world, regardless of whether it is predominantly cold or hot. The only places it avoids are those where the water freezes, because then there is a shortage of food. If it sees the probability of water freezing in a particular place, it abandons that spot just prior [to its freezing]. It does so with the help of its rather advanced deductive powers. Thus, if in any particular location it is seen that the cranes are leaving, it can be deduced that very cold weather is coming in the near future, just as it can be known that the rainy season is imminent when the cátaka [swallows] are seen flying westwards at the end of the hot season.

The rainy season begins a day or two after the rain clouds reach the Bengal coastal region from the Bay of Bengal. The cátaka bird is native to Africa. In the spring it crosses over the Arabian Sea and the southern peninsula and enters Bengal. It remains in Bengal during the summer. Once the monsoon starts, it heads westward, crosses back over the Arabian Sea and returns to its homeland – Africa.
As with the crane, this deductive power is highly developed in the egret. Some people call it intuition. Be that as it may, the crane is native to this country. ( 10 )

In ancient times in the central part of Bengal, in the deserted part of the River Mathabhanga, a huge watershed was created. It was a reservoir full of fish. Many mango trees surrounded the reservoir. A flock of cranes used to sit in these trees and spend their days eating fish in the watershed. Due to the overcrowding of these cranes, the place came to be known as Bagula – in spoken Bengali, Boglá. Another place in Báuṋgálisthán was Boguŕá – in spoken language, Bogŕá. In English it was called “Bogŕe”, in Bengali it was spelled Baguŕá. The place in Nadia district I am speaking of is Bagula; even now the elderly people call it Boglá. It is no longer a village; today it is a small town.

Be that as it may, you are well acquainted with the crane. The crane will sit silently, its beak lowered for hours at a time, beside any body of water. It appears as if absorbed in some sort of meditation. Actually, it is not. In reality it is silently sitting there, fixing its gaze on the fish. Lest the fish become alert at the sound of its wings, it continues to maintain that silence. If any person makes a false show of their piousness, or when one in reality is planning something otherwise, we call them vakadhármika [like a crane falsely appearing to be pious]. If any of you are “falsely pious like a crane”, show your true face and let the people know who you are.

The indigenous crane is usually of a pearly white colour. Of course, on the other side of the Himalayas in Tibet, outer Mongolia and Siberia, there are cranes of butter oil colour and of a pale yellow colour. Compared to the Indian cranes, they are slightly smaller in appearance. Each has a small crest on its head. These cranes are very fond of sport. While gathering food, they devote their time for the necessary period, sitting beside the water, lying in wait for unsuspecting fish. Thereafter they become wholly engaged in playing with other cranes. But the use of the word “falsely pious” with reference to these kinds of cranes would not be appropriate. To lay their eggs they come down to the plains in the waterlogged areas of India surrounded by forests, and they settle down there temporarily. At the end of winter, with their little ones in tow – the babies have by this time learned to fly – they cross over to their original home beyond the Himalayas. ( 11 )

Swan: Most birds belonging to the swan genus are not permanent residents of India. The rájahaḿsa or Indian swans, although they belong to the swan genus, have hardly any ability to fly. The swans we see during the winter are residents of cold countries. To escape from the cold weather and to lay eggs, they come to the comparatively warmer climates of countries like India. These birds come during winter to the Sundarbans of Bengal, to the Kaziranga forest areas of Assam, the wetlands between the Barak and Surma Rivers of Cachar [Assam], Chalanbil of North Bengal, Hizali Bill of Ráŕh, ma-an of Bettiah, (in Bihar the wetland or bill is called ma – a – n), to the ma – an of Lakhandei River near Muzaffarpur, Unnao district of Uttar Pradesh, Bharatpur area of Rajasthan and the region close to the small Rhann of Kucch. They fly at a great height so that hunters cannot kill them easily. ( 12 )

Flamingo: The meaning of karaka is a certain type of bird from cold countries that normally comes to India from the end of the month of Karttik [late autumn] to the end of the month of Mágh [winter] and makes temporary nests in areas near different reservoirs and ponds. These guest birds usually make their nests in the tall trees near reservoirs and ponds. They are the old inhabitants of northeast China, Siberia, Russia and Tibet, but due to the oppressive cold in those lands during wintertime it becomes impossible for them to sustain themselves. It is extremely cold, and moreover there is a scarcity of food. Thus they come to India and other hot countries during the winter and remain there for a few months. During this time they lay their eggs, and after their young are somewhat grown they teach them how to fly and how to gather food. Then, when the hot winds begin to blow, they return to their homeland. They return to the exact place they came from, and every year they again return to the same place. By attaching a marker to their legs or through other means, their incredibly- developed intuition and ability to recognize places has been verified. Great crowds of [these flamingos] gather during winter in the Kolkata Zoo, Sandeshkhali of 24 Paraganas, and Bharatpurʼs bird sanctuary. At one time, great numbers of them used to come to Dimdiha village in Purulia District [in Anandanagar]. Since they came here to lay their eggs [d́im], the name of that place became D́imdihá. They can be seen in the marshlands of Bengal during wintertime. Karaka refers to the birds of this flamingo family. ( 13 )

Diver bird (pánkaoŕi): Karkat́a is a bird of the kot́ik (kaoŕi) family. When we mention the kot́ika bird family, what is generally seen in Bengal, is the páńkaoŕi [the diver bird, similar to a cormorant]. At one time the diver bird was found in good number in large reservoirs, ponds and marshlands of Bengal. This tri-habitat bird (aquatic, terrestrial and aerial) is similar in nature to the swan or goose. Its body is a blackish colour. Like other non-Indian birds, they are seen in good number in Bengal during the winter season, but also remain there at other times. The author saw flocks of diver birds in Murshidabad Districtʼs Hizalbil during the winter of 1942. One hears that there are not so many pánkaoŕis nowadays. They have been and are still being slaughtered by human beings.

According to the Puranas, just as the mount of the goddess Gauṋgá is the makara [a mythological aquatic creature like the crocodile], similarly Yamunaʼs mount is the pánikot́ika, or pánkaoŕi. According to some of the Puranas, the mount of the god of machines, Vishvakarmá, is also the pánkaoŕi. However there is a difference of opinion about this. ( 14 )

Migratory bird of the rainy season (cátaka, phiuṋe): Kokila is a word which stands for the Banzalitis (Bánglá or Bánjálá, Latin adjective, Banzalitis) group of phiuṋe birds [fork-tailed birds]. However, in Sanskrit the Banjalities group of birds are not merely called kokila, rather they are called Bauṋga kokila. The original habitat of the phiuṋe or fork-tailed bird is Bengal. Of course, today they are found in all parts of India except the hottest and coldest regions. Usually they do not go outside India even for a change of weather. If at all they migrate, it will be only a brief journey.

Birds that arrive in India during winter are not looked upon as Indian birds. We consider them as birds that have arrived to lay eggs. After laying their eggs, they again return to their homeland. There are one or two exceptions, however. The swallow (cátaka), for instance, is an exception. It is a bird of African origin. Normally at the end of winter it crosses the Arabian sea to India and stays for the spring and summer seasons. As the monsoon air arrives from the Bay of Bengal, the cátaka [swallow], with its natural intuition, understands and before the rainy season starts and the monsoon air blows, it begins its journey back home. With the return of the swallow, the ornithologists understand that in a week or maximum ten days time, the rainy season will begin. The phiuṋe are found to cross over the northern part of the Bay of Bengal; they do not like to go often to the southern part. So in the Andamans, the phiuṋe of Indian species are scarcely found. The phiuṋe of Indonesian variety are found in the Nicobar islands. Phiuṋe are not ferocious like doels. ( 15 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Parrot, Cockatoo: You surely must be aware of the fact that talking birds are by common consensus divided into two groups: one group is called shuk, and the other group is known as sárii or sáriká. These two groups of birds are talking birds. The beaks of the birds, called shuk, are thick at the source and thin or pointed at the end; they are curved. The beaks of shuks are generally red in colour. Of course, there are some birds of the shuk group whose beaks are not exactly red in colour. Our family birds like t́iyá [parrot], ban-tiyá [wild parrot], candaná [a kind of parrot having red streaks around its throat] and kákátuá (cockatoo) all belong to the shuk group. They appear to be green, yellowish-green or white in outward appearance. Owls do not come out in the day time. Yet, they are similar in appearance to the shuk birds. Owls, however, are not talking birds. Shuks are called sugá in Urdu. The exquisitely red beak of the shuk became sweet indeed in the poetʼs imagination. When looking at the lush red colour of palásh [Butea monosperma] blossoms in the spring, a question arose in the poetʼs mind as to whether it was really a flower or the red beak of the shuk bird. Speaking in Sanskrit, the poet asked, “Was it shuk?” “Kiḿ Shuka?” So from Sanskrit the flower came to be known as kiḿshuka.
Among these talking birds, the parrot, the wild parrot and candaná belong to eastern India, and in particular are the local birds of Bengal. The cockatoo is a bird that comes from outside India.

The beak of birds belonging to the sárii group is straight and pointed. Our indigenous myna ( 1 ) were the primary species among the birds of the sárii category. Its original habitat was eastern India, especially Ráŕh and Orissa. Millions [of these birds] thrived in the forests of Midnapur, Bhanjabhum, Bankura and Birbhum. The parrot, the wild parrot, the wild myna or pied myna belong to the shuk category of birds. Of course they cannot talk like the mynas. Mynas also have a well developed vocabulary. They articulate many words among themselves.

The quarrelling among the shálikhs [small, yellow beak birds of the house-myna species] is indeed worth watching. In South Bengal, in the wetlands surrounded by small patches of marshland, there once lived many shálikhs [sárii group] in a big banyan tree, due to which the village came to be known as Shálikhá. It is now an important part of Howrah town. Some people erroneously call this area Salkia. This mistake should be corrected.

Our familiar birds – the bábui (weaver-bird, báyá ciŕiá in Urdu), t́unt́uni (tailor bird in English, in Urdu julhá-ciŕiyá), bulbuli (in English nightingale, in Urdu bulbul) – they all belong to the sárii group. Those of you who are familiar with Vaeśńava literature must have heard or read the narrative of Shuk-Sárii called Krśńakathá related to Rádhá and Krśńa. Among the talking birds of Bengal, the candaná belonging to the shuk group and the myna belonging to the sárii group are more gifted than other birds. During the last fifty years, thousands of birds have been exported abroad from Tripura, Midnapur and Bhanjabhum. India is becoming devoid of myna birds. I am drawing the attention of everyone to this development. Candaná are normally very limited in number. Their numbers are continuing to diminish. Perhaps they are also being secretly exported abroad.

There was a time when most people belonging to the middle class along with wealthy families used to keep birds as pets in their houses. They normally kept myna or candaná as pets. These two kinds of birds are very calm and quiet. Cockatoos are also talented talking birds. However, they are comparatively larger in size. Their attitude is quite aggressive. That is why they are kept chained to a stand. During the Moghul period even the parrots and candaná were kept chained to a stand. Today they are simply kept in cages. The number of birds is rapidly diminishing. Due to a dearth of money, householders are giving up many of their luxurious habits. Like the dodo birds, these other birds are also awaiting their final days. ( 2 )

Myna, Magpie Robin: Mynas are talking birds. An entity which speaks its own language and also utters the words of others, that is, speaks various words, is known as harabolá [capable of mimicking various voices]. The word har [various] comes from the Persian language. In between the house myna and myna there is a bird species that the villagers of Burdwan district call guye myná or guye nyákŕá [wild myna]. These can also be trained to talk. Normally people do not keep wild mynas as pets, but they do keep other mynas. In Sanskrit mynas are called sáriká. Among the more familiar birds of Ráŕh are mynas, red-throated parrots and cockatoos.

Among the birds belonging to the parrot order, there are cockatoos of different colours – light-green, yellowish, with specks in the throat – candanás of normal appearance and green, hefty parrots, wild parrots and the green-coloured magpie robin (doyel) of Bengal, which are commonly seen in northern Bengal and rarely seen in southern Bengal. Of this group, candanás prefer to stay away from human localities; cockatoos prefer to stay in a humid environment at a distance from such localities. Wild parrots remain in the forest and fly over human localities. They rarely rest at any particular spot. Magpie robins live close to settled habitats, always moving in search of insects. They are very cruel and ferocious in nature.

Amongst all these, candanás and cockatoos are talking birds. Magpie robins are not talking birds, but their notes are very sweet. Parrots and wild parrots do not have sweet notes, but are very impressive in appearance. In Sanskrit the parrot is called shuk, and their beaks are scarlet-red in colour like ripe telakucás [vegetables like the wax gourd but without stripes]. There is a couplet [a riddle] about the pineapple which says, “From the forest emerges the parrot, with a golden crown on its head.” ( 3 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Pigeon: By kapota we mean pigeon. From the word kapota comes the word kabutar, and from the word párávat is derived the word páyrá. Kapotaraka > kaotara > kautar > kabutara. By adding the suffix kan to kapota we form the word kapotaka. The word kapota refers to any aircraft, but the word kapotaka means pigeon and nothing else. The etymological meaning of grha kapota is any domesticated pigeon. In common usage it refers to house pigeon or golá páyrá. In ancient times, the people of Ráŕh had boundless affection for birds and animals. To prevent people from flaying the skin of dead animals, they even used to dig pits near the path by their home to bury the corpses of dead animals [cows and other animals] so that no one could come to flay their skin secretly or carry away their flesh by digging them out. To prevent hawks and greedy persons from killing the pigeons, local people, while constructing their mud homes, used to insert clay pitchers at a slant in the wall. Pigeons could use the pitchersʼ opening as an entrance to reach their nests inside. I do not know if this is done nowadays, but they used to do it earlier. Since pigeons lived in homes, they were called grha kapota [domesticated pigeons] or golá páyrá. They were so called because they used to live on the paddy corns of the corn bin in houses. ( 1 )

Ka means “water”, pota means “ship”. That which does a shipʼs work at the time of crossing a large reservoir, lake or sea is kapota. That is its etymological meaning. The colloquial meaning of the word kapota is ghugu [“dove”] and páyrá [“pigeon”]. In olden days, when roads were not well-developed, people used to send messages to distant lands with the help of trained pigeons or doves. Generally a letter was attached to one of the birdʼs limbs. Once those trained doves or pigeons arrived at their destination, they would then carry back a reply. This system of mail delivery with the help of these birds was prevalent for many years on the battlefield. Pigeon post was even used in some places in India during British rule. From this word kapota or kapotaraka we obtain the word kabutara (in Mymensingh Bengali, kaetara). However, for “pigeon” the word páyrá is better than the word kabutara, because páyrá has come from the Sanskrit word párávata. Párávata refers only to “pigeon” and not to “dove”, but kapota means both “pigeon” and “dove”. The feminine form of kapota is kapotii; another meaning of kapotii is “a small, ocean-going vessel”.

The original home of our well-known domesticated pigeon (golá páyrá) is Bengal, but the non-domesticated pigeon (lakká páyrá) came from elsewhere. The dodo bird, which disappeared from the earth approximately one hundred years ago due to the malevolence of human beings, evolved from this domesticated pigeon.

People scatter kernels of grain in front of pigeons, or on their usual path, for them to eat. This scattering is called “pigeon feeding.” At the end of autumn, when the paddy fields are somewhat muddy, seeds are scattered in those paddy fields where it is not possible to sow seeds for the winter season, or where, due to lack of water, those seeds will not sprout in the dead of winter even if sown. These sprout and grow into plants in the spaces between the paddy. When the paddy is harvested, the tops of these plants are also cut. As a result, more branches grow, and at the end of the cold season they yield a generous amount of flowers and pods. This type of seed-scattered crop is called the “pyra crop” [pigeon-harvest]. Small lentils, gram or blackish-coloured small gram [also called t́hikre cholá], pea [blackish-coloured, small pea, also called t́hikre mat́ar], rapeseed, khesári or teoŕá (triput́ii or triput́iká – Lathirus sativas) – these crops are generally produced as part of the pyra crop. In most parts of Bihar, the pyra cropping is called páyruyá. On land where there is no system of irrigation, or where the soil becomes hard or cracked at the end of winter, the produce from the pyra cropping is of great benefit to the farmers. Moreover, this pyra crop increases the soilʼs fertility and productivity. As for the surplus, the stalks, pod husks and chaff make excellent bird food and cattle fodder. If mustard is planted, it yields oil cake which can be used as both fertilizer and bird food.

Although it is slightly off the topic, it is worth mentioning that, as far as possible, it is better not to feed pigeons by scattering wheat grains, because in many peopleʼs opinion, pigeons may contract dysentery if they eat too much wheat grain [gam]. Godhúma > gohúma > gaham > gam. The word gaham is prevalent in western Ráŕh and Orissa. That river water which is transparent like the eyes of a pigeon is called kapotákśa in masculine gender and kapotákśii in feminine gender. Michael Madhusudhan Datta was born in Sagardáṋri village, which is situated on the bank of the Kapotákśii River in Jessore District. ( 2 )

Peacock: The peacock (mayúr) is a special bird of India. Its original habitat is Southeast Asia. The male peacock can spread its tail and dance; the female peacock has no tail and never dances. It is also ugly to look at. It generally prefers a dry climate, and cannot lay eggs in a humid environment. There may be peacocks in damp forest areas, but for laying eggs they move away to distant drier climates. In Bengal, rather in eastern India, there are few peacocks in the forest areas due to excessive rain. In the Bankura and Purulia districts of western Ráŕh, some peacocks are found in the forests because of the dry climate. Due to the dry climate in western India, especially in Rajasthan and Gujarat, peacocks abound.

There are generally three different types of peacocks: (1) Our very familiar, colourful peacocks, (2) yellowish peacocks, and (3) white peacocks from Burma and Thailand (Shyámdesh). White peacocks can somehow tolerate a humid environment. Another name for peacock is shikhii. The call of the peacock is known as keká. Hence the word keká means peacock. In ancient times the peacock was a favorite food item for human beings. Emperor Ashoka did not entirely forbid the butchering of peacocks in his kitchen, even after his transformation into Dharmáshoka [non-violent or Buddhist Ashoka].

Mayúr is originally a Sanskrit word; the feminine of mayúr is mayúrii. The Hindi translation of the word is mor; its feminine form is morni. The meat of the female peacock tastes bitter. That is why normally people never kill female peacocks. Today the peacock has been given recognition as the national bird of India. ( 3 )

Crow: The verbal root kae means “to give a dreadful shout” or “to give an ear-splitting cry”. By adding the suffix kan to the verbal root kae, we obtain the word káka, whose etymological meaning is “one who shouts in an ugly manner”. Bhola Mayra [a literary character] has said – “If the cawing of crows and the beating of drums cease, it is good.”

There are many colloquial meanings of the word káka, the ordinary crow that we commonly see. According to biologists, the crow is not a very old bird. This half-carnivorous bird (it has an equal fondness for both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food) is renowned for its intelligence. In Bihar it is said, manukhme (one writes it as mánuś but pronounces it manukh) naová, ciṋŕai me kaová. [“Among humans the barber, and among birds the crow.”] That is, among human beings, the most intelligent are the barbers; among birds it is the crow. Their solidarity is also praiseworthy.

The solidarity of crows is indeed laudable. If someone kills a single crow, then within a short period of time a great number of crows will gather there and try to collectively harass the killer. When crows gather somewhere in a group, that assembly of crows is also called káka, but the word for this assembly of crows is feminine plural, that is, kákáh (like the plural form of latá). ( 4 )
Perhaps you know that crows are generally of three types – (1) general crow, (2) jackdaw (raven), and (3) white crow.

You might have seen general crows very often in the streets and on the rooftop and courtyard of your house. Jackdaws are fewer in number, somewhat larger in size and black in colour. Their voice is extremely harsh… something like ka, ka, ka (kka). Their beaks are a little longer and harder than those of general crows. The colour of white crows is not exactly white; rather, it is grey. In ancient times, white crows used to be called báyasa. Nowadays báyasa means any type of crow. In northern India crows are called kaová, and jackdaws are called kág. In Auṋgiká language, jackdaws are called dṋáŕkaová. In the language of Ráŕh, Bengal, they are called ko or koy.

Crows make many hard food items edible by pecking. They can very easily pierce the meat of any animal into pieces and eat it. Hence all species of crows are called khat́akhádaka. Crows have absolutely no prejudice against any type of food. Hence they will even eat something that is unfit for consumption (in Sanskrit, called kákánna).

The second meaning of khat́akhádaka is byághra (vi – a – ghra + a = byághra) or tiger. That is, an animal whose sense of smell is very strong. If a tiger gets a promising scent, it easily locates the prey and pounces on it. Just as a crow is termed a khat́akhádaka due to the strength of its beak, so also a tiger is called a khat́akhádaka by virtue of its strong claws and teeth. Another characteristic of the tiger is that, simply by supposition, it makes a calculated leap so as to fall exactly on its prey.

Another meaning of the word khat́akhádaka is sheyál or jackal (synonymous words are shrgál, shibá, jambuka). Jackals will eat the rotten meat that even vultures are averse to eating. Hence jackals are also famous as khat́akhádaka.

Even in the case of human beings, you will come across some who are khat́akhádaka. Just go to a fish market at the peak of the rainy season and you will see many gentlemen buying rotten hilsas. Are these human beings in any way superior to jackals? Hence for this kind of person, you can certainly use the word khat́akhádaka. You will sometimes find certain ladies cutting freshwater barbel and catfish in a very cruel manner…, breaking the claws of a Chilka lake lobster, stabbing young anabas and twisting and wringing them ruthlessly. They are, of course, ladies, but they are certainly khat́akhádaka. ( 5 )

Owl and Crow: Kákári: Káka + ari = kákári. Kákasya arih ityarthe kákárih (śaśt́ii tatpuruśa samása ( 6 ). Ari means “enemy”. Thus the etymological meaning of kákári is “owl”. Owls (pecá or pecaka) cannot see during the day. If a crow spies an owl during the day it will peck at it. Fearful of crows, the owl hides itself in the dark crevices of trees during the day. Crows cannot see at night, so if an owl sees a crow at night it attacks it. But since crows have more strength in their beaks than owls they save themselves somehow. Thus, it is seen that it is the crowʼs young that are generally killed by owls. If an owl is not overly hungry it will not eat crow-meat. Since the crowʼs meat is bad-tasting, no bird will eat it apart from the vulture. It is said that the crow eats any kind of meat, but it also will not eat crow-meat. ( 7 )

Cuckoo (Kokil): By adding the suffix itch to ka we obtain the word kil. Ko + kil = kokil, which refers to something that announces its identity through sound. This is its etymological meaning. Still, in common parlance kokil [the cuckoo] is a particular type of black bird. Kokil > ko – i – l > koyel. Its synonym is pik and paravrta, or that which dwells in anotherʼs home [nest]. The word pik indicates the cooing of the bird, even the bird itself. A comparative observation is:
Pik kibá kuiṋje kuiṋje kuhu kuhu gáy;
Phule phule d́hale paŕe áji kina madhu báy.
[The cuckoo coos in the bowers, while on the flowers a sweet breeze blows.]

The story goes that the cuckoo is unable to give warmth to its eggs. So in the absence of the crow, it goes to the crowʼs nest and lays its eggs there. The crow mistakenly treats the cuckooʼs eggs as its own, provides them warmth and takes care of them. When the young appear, breaking through their shells and beginning to cry, the sound of the cuckoo is noticed. When the crow realizes that it has mistakenly taken care of young babies not its own, it drives them out of the nest. That is why the crow which tends the children of others is called paravrta and the cuckoo is also called paravrta because it has been looked after by others. In this context it should be remembered that the sweet cooing of the cuckoo is done by the male bird in the spring season, not by the the female cuckoo (kokilá). In one Hindi poem it is said: koeli nahi bolti hái. [The female cuckoo does not sing.] In reality, during the rainy season it is the dardoor [male frog] that calls and not the darduri or dáduri, although in one song it is said, dáke dáduri [the female frog sings].

One song says, náce mayúrii, dáke dáduri [The peahen dances and the female frog sings.] This is not true. It applies to all sorts of frogs: kolá vyáuṋg, sońá vyáuṋg, kuńo vyáuṋg, kat́kat́e vyáuṋg and flying frogs. The female frog looks on calmly; it is the male frog that swells its wind pipe and cries loudly.
The feminine gender of kokil is kokilá, not kokili, although in the feminine gender in Hindi it is koeli. ( 8 )

Shyámá bird: Shyámá is the name of a small bird [a song bird of the thrush family] that we find in Bengal as well as eastern India. Although this small bird is not very beautiful to look at, its voice is very attractive. The name of this bird is also káliká. Satyendranath Datta writes in one of his poems:
Kotháy dáke doyel-shyámá
Phiuṋe gáche gáche náce re,
Kotháy jale marál cale
Marálii tár piche piche.
[Where do you find that place where doyel, shyámá sing, And fork-tailed birds dance on the branches of a tree? Where is that place where the swan glides? And the goose follows from behind?] ( 9 )]

Sparrow: The meaning of the word grhacát́aka is sparrow or caŕuii bird. Cát́aka > cad́a-a > cad́ái > caŕái; cát́akii >cad́a-i > cad́ui > caŕui. In Bengali both the words cat́ái and caŕui are in use. In western Ráŕh, most people in rural areas call the bird cat́ui. The word cat́ui comes from the word cat́aka. In the Magahii language of Bihar it is called garbaiyá. In Maithili also it is called garbaiyá or sometime phuddi. In Bhojpuri it is called phurguddi. The sparrow is divided into two groups: those that build nests in the cornices of wealthy houses called grhacát́aka or sparrows. Sparrows cannot build their nests carefully and neatly with straw and dry grass as pigeons do.

In the world of birds, the largest ones – the eagles and the condors – also cannot build their nests. Although belonging to the eagle group but comparatively smaller in appearance, Indian vultures somehow build their resting places on the thicker branches of large trees. Smaller birds like weaver birds build strong nests. They usually build their nests on palm trees or on the higher branches of tall trees. Tailor birds also build strong nests by stitching up the leaves of trees with their beaks. Both pigeons and sparrows, since they are incapable of building their nests [in trees], have their resting places in the crevices of rocks or hills. Titir or partridge birds also do the same, although they somehow manage to build lower quality homes for themselves in the cornices of wealthy houses.
Bábui pákhire dáki baliche caŕái
Kuŕe ghare theke karo shilper baŕái.
Ámi tháki mahásukhe at́t́áliká pare
Tumi kata kaśt́a páo rod brśt́i jhaŕe.
Bábui hásiyá kahe sandeha ki táy
Kaśt́a pái tabu tháki niijer vásáy.
Páká hok tabu bhái parer se vásá
Niija háte gaŕá mor kácá ghar khásá.

[Calling to the weaver bird the sparrow says: Staying in a hut, you boast of your weaving skill. I live in great happiness in the palace. You suffer so much in sunshine, storm and rain. The weaving bird laughs and says, ‘No doubt, I may suffer, yet I live in my own house. Even your palace belongs to another, This house built by me is rough but fine, as it is mine’.]

The wild sparrows that do not stay in houses live instead in small trees close to paddy fields. The primary activity of these birds is to pick up and eat whatever remnants of crops remain in the fields after harvesting. In Bengal there are very few swallow species. In the winter, they arrive in limited numbers from western countries after the paddy is harvested. They live close to the paddy fields in small trees. They stay for a fortnight or more and then return to the west.

The people of rural Bengal call them bon caŕui [wild sparrow]. Greedy people say that the meat of these birds is very delicious; so they trap them from behind with nets and slay them. Their number is thus gradually dwindling. They are so small that even by killing a hundred wild sparrows a man will not be able to satisfy his appetite. They should be saved from the onslaught of men. In India they are also called bagaerii. In the Bhojpuri language also they are called bagaerii:
Jaisan dareli báj se bagaerii.
[As a wild sparrow is frightened at the sight of a falcon.] ( 10 )]
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Ducks and Chickens: Ke + ru + ac = Keraba. The word ke means “in water”. The verb ru means to make noise in joy. So the word koeraba means the bird that makes noise when submerged in water. Keraba means “ducks” (pátiháṋs). When they come across water, they run and utter joyful sounds like ‘quack, quack’. In this connection, we should remember that although the Bengali word háṋs has come from the Sanskrit word haḿsa, in Sanskrit the word haḿsa does not refer to any particular species of duck; it refers only to the swan (rájhaḿsa). For swan there is another word in Sanskrit, marál, which is now known to belong to the flamingo group. For different species of ducks (háṋs) familiar to us, the Sanskrit name is keraba; for the swan, marál or Haḿsa. In Sanskrit the use of the word rájhaḿsa is very limited; rather, it is hardly used. For duck, the word keraba is used, and for another variety of duck, that is, for the Chinese duck (ciiná patiháṋs), the Sanskrit word is krśńa-keraba or piuṋgal keraba. For sand-coloured duck (báli háṋs), the name used is baláká [a small goose capable of flying high].

Although the technical title for Chinese duck is ciiná pátiháṋs, the phrase is self-contradictory. The word páti refers to anything indigenous. So how can anything indigenous to India be Chinese? This is very much like the word ‘lemon-indica’ or ‘lemon banjalitis,’ which in Bengal is called páti nebu. This slightly elongated lemon with sweet-smelling skin that we call kágjii nebu has come from overseas. Some kágjii Muslims of the Hoogly district of West Bengal were engaged in the business of producing a thick, ancient variety of paper called kágaz. After their traditional occupations were ruined, they went to South America and brought the elongated lemon back with them to India. Since it was a group of kágjii Muslims that brought these lemons to India, they have come to be known as kágjii nebu.

Towards the end of the Moghul period, a particular kind of duck brought from China has come to be known as ciiná háṋs. They lay more eggs than the indigenous ducks. There is very little expenditure in keeping indigenous ducks. All that is required is some food for the ducklings and a room to keep them safe from snakes, mongooses and jackals. This takes very little expense. The maintenance of the Chinese duck is quite similar, although not identical. Chinese ducks are quite prone to disease – at the slightest infection they die in droves. The jackals, of course, make an inroad on the duck population, but only when they get opportunity and time. However, they do pay more attention to the Chinese ducks. Hence to maintain Chinese ducks, the owner has to be additionally concerned about their safety. For these reasons, despite their yielding a greater quantity of eggs, the domestication of Chinese ducks never became popular. In contrast, the people of Bengal have been keeping indigenous ducks for at least three thousand years.

Unlike maintaining hens, there is very little risk in keeping indigenous ducks. Since they do not eat up any vegetation, there is no danger of getting involved in quarrels with the neighbours. They do not enter the houses and make them dirty, since they are drawn only to the water.

The Ráŕh region of Bengal is a land of sticky [clay] soil. Hence the ponds of that area have greater capacity to retain water, and there are greater numbers of these ponds. Due to the easy availability of these ponds, keeping ducks has been a very popular practice in present day Ráŕh, what to speak of ancient Ráŕh.

The presence of ducks, unlike that of hens, has never been detrimental to the health of householders. For this reason people have always built a room for ducks near the doorstep. In the morning the doors are thrown open, and the ducks immediately run to the ponds. The resident then retrieves the eggs from their room. We experienced this regularly in our childhood days.

In ancient Bengal, although there were plenty of wild hens, cocks and waterfowl, people rarely kept hens (murgii) at home, chiefly because the hens made the houses and courtyards dirty, ate up the neighboursʼ plants and trees, and ate repulsive offal before the very eyes of their owners. Of course, the people of Bengal also hunted wild cocks and hens in those days. Wild cocks can fly; even the domesticated fowl can fly to an extent, but certain ducks are unable to fly. So it is quite convenient for people to keep ducks. For the indigenous ducks it is also convenient because otherwise their lives would have been endangered.

Most birds belonging to the class of flamingos or geese can fly well – they can fly ceaselessly for several hundred miles. Despite also belonging to that class, the common duck cannot fly. Hence by maintaining geese, only the geese themselves are benefited. People are hardly benefited because goose eggs are very hot and are hence unpopular. They also lay fewer eggs.

Wild cocks are primarily birds that fly in the sky, while ducks are birds that live in water or at times are amphibious – they live in water as well as on land. Both geese and ducks eat water insects and moss and keep the ponds clean. From that point of view, geese and ducks have an important role to play in the rural ecology.

Those who keep geese, ducks and Chinese ducks must ensure that there are no big holes or ditches around the ponds in which jackals might live. I do not want jackals to be destroyed as a species. Let them live near the river beds or in the forests; but if they reside on the banks of ponds, the lives of ducks are endangered. People who keep ducks in their home should always have some lime and turmeric paste handy. When the jackals attack the ducks and leave them behind after a chase, the application of lime and turmeric paste helps the wounded ducks to survive. ( 1 )

The word koke stands for ducklings. You all know that most birds peck at crumbs of food or grains. So, most of them belong to the group called koke. This word properly applies to ducks and especially to ducklings. They eat more food than required and hence, many ducklings die of stomach ailments.

This also applies to hens, especially their little ones. Due to excessive eating, and indiscriminate intake of food that is unfit for consumption, they often have epidemics of stomach ailments. In a short time, due to such epidemics, villages can loose their entire hen population.

Those who keep hens or ducks must pay strict attention to this habit of overeating by the chicks and ducklings. Sometimes, thousands of them are involved. They must see to it that the little ones do not eat any kind of food indiscriminately. The chicks and ducklings should be given tender leaves and only little snails to eat; big snails must not be given to them as food. They must not be given grains of paddy; only when they are slightly grown up can they be given paddy grains. Wheat grains should not be given to hens or ducks of any age. Ducks, hens and pigeons can suffer from diarrhea due to eating wheat grains. ( 2 )

Primitive Mammoth: In English, the word for aerávat is mammoth. You certainly describe a large meeting as a “mammoth meeting”. This mammoth was a prehistoric animal. Their descendants are the elephants. In the world today, among the various elephant species the largest one is the African elephant. It is somewhat lacking in intelligence, but is quite huge in height. It is surmised that the primitive mammoth was twice the size of these African elephants. Their tusk was quite long. This huge animal, lacking in intelligence, became extinct nearly half a million years ago. Fossils of this creature have been found in certain areas of Bankura and Purulia. Others have even been found in the eastern part of Ranchi district in the Suvarnarekha Valley. In any case, from what we have come to know thus far, after the primitive dinosaur, these mammoths were the largest creatures to appear on earth. In other words, they were the “second-order” animals in the animal kingdom. Still, it must be remembered that mammoths and dinosaurs did not belong to the same period. Dinosaurs were more primitive than mammoths. In addition, among dinosaurs, the huge-sized dinosaurs (mainly vegetarian) were more primitive than the smaller (mainly non-vegetarian) dinosaurs. ( 1 ) It is surmised that since they were food for the smaller dinosaurs, these huge mammoths became extinct long ago. The smaller-sized dinosaurs became extinct during an Ice Age, most probably under the cover of snow.

t: Yes, I was speaking of the aerávats (mammoths). “Risen from the sea” – if that is the etymological meaning of “mammoths” – then in that sense, whatever comes from the sea can be called aerávats, however small or large they might be in appearance.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The imaginary páriját flowers, the imaginary amrta (nectar), aerávat and Puranic Mahálakśmii, are also, in that sense aerávat. Again, the silakantha, or primitive fish, and todayʼs conch shells, octopus and iodine, in that sense also belong to the category of aerávat; but in common usage only mammoths are aerávats and no one else. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Elephants are endangered animals: In ancient times, in various countries of the world, there were several types of elephants (hátii) of different colours and species. Now, because of deforestation, the habitats of elephants have been reduced, more or less, to Africa and India. In addition, in the northern and western parts of India, elephants are nearly extinct. They exist only in the southern and eastern parts of India. To the south, in Andhra Pradesh (adjacent to Orissa), in Karnataka, and in some parts of Kerala they are still found. In the highly crowded state of Kerala there are few forests. Earlier, when there were ample forests, tall and handsome elephants lived there. Some of these elephants could be found in the well-known forest reserves of Tekkari in Kerala. In the state of Karnataka, there was once a predominance of elephants.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Until recently, elephants were caught with the help of improvised traps (khedás). However, in Orissa there was no such practice of catching elephants. In the mountainous parts of Orissa, better known as Koshal, there were once a good number of elephants; their population had diminished; but now, with Government protection, their numbers are rising.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: In Bihar, in the Ráŕh region of Bengal, there were large numbers of elephants. Due to fear of elephants during autumn and winter, people used to light fires outside their homes to scare them away. Today there are still elephants in Bhanjabhum in Ráŕh, in Dhalbhum, in Jhargram, in the southwestern part of Bankura, in some areas of the north Midnapur Sadar (main), in Purulia, and in the hilly areas of Seraikella and Dalma. There were once plenty of elephants, even mammoths, in the Jaicandi hills of Purulia, in the hills of Tilabani, in the Panchakot hills, and in the hills of Sushunia and Beharinath (according to some, Beharilal). I once saw fossils of mammoths in these areas. The age of mammoths came to an end several million years ago. Although the elephant era still continues, there are no elephants in those regions today. In the hills of Purulia, Ayodhya, Taherbera, and especially Jabar, there remain some elephants, which enter the villages during winter in search of ripe paddy and maize.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: In the northern parts of West Bengal, in Coochbehar, Jalpaiguri, Siliguri, and in the forest areas of Goalpara, the number of large elephants and their dominion was quite impressive. Today their number has dwindled almost into non-existence. Nevertheless, a few of them remain. In Meghalaya, in the northern part of Maymansingh, in the northern part of Sylhet district, everywhere in Cachhar district, in the Nowgong and Karbiang, there were once plenty of elephants. They belong to the species of small elephants that are very clever.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: One feels uneasy upon realizing that once upon a time, in the forest of Naritabari, Sarisabari, Susanga and Bhawal [in Bangladesh], hordes of elephants used to roam. Even until the end of the Moghul period, elephants of smaller size were in abundance in Tripura. After the battle between the King of Tripura and the Moghul emperor, the ruler of Tripura offered elephants as a gift to the emperor.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Since the forests of Tripura have been reduced, the number of elephants there has also diminished. Some elephants are still found in Mizoram, Manipur, along the borders of Nagaland, Arunachal, and the Brahmaputra valley of Assam. They are quite large in size. They now heave a sigh of relief after the creation of the Kaziranga forest reserves. They have also been saved to some extent from the khedá operations, that is, improvised traps set by poachers inside the jungles to capture elephants.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Since ancient times, Assam or Prágjyotiśpur or Kamrup was quite famous for its elephants. That is why in ancient Sanskrit literature, Kamrup was not only known as Kámákhyádhám but also as Gajadhám [land of the elephant]. In Assam even today, khedá operations are carried out. In one of my earlier discourses I mentioned that at one time, elephants were bought and sold throughout the year, but particularly during Kárttik Purńimá at the Hariharkśetra fair (in Hazipur district of Bihar). Nowadays there are more people wanting to sell their elephants, but only a few people interested to purchase them. In Gajadhám (Kamrup) at one time the number of elephants decreased substantially. I am now told that it has risen slightly. Still, compared to other parts of India, the number of elephants in Kamrup is appreciably more than that of other places.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: At one time hordes of elephants used to move about in the forests of western Ráŕh, especially in the forests of the adjoining hills and hillocks (duḿri). Although the number of elephants has been reduced, they are still quite prevalent. Of course, their number is greater in the forests of Jhargram, Bhanjabhum and Dhalbhum, in Jabar Hills, Dalma Hills, and in the areas adjoining the Ayodhya Hills. When elephants make an inroad into the villages in quest of ripe paddy and maize, the villagers kneel down with folded hands and say their prayers:

t: Nature of elephants: Fools can be divided into several groups: “absolute fool”, “ignorant fool”, “blatant fool”, “solid fool”, “elephant-fool” (hastimúrkha), and some people even say “cow-fool” (go-múrkha). The word gańd́a-múrkha means someone whose foolishness has reached down to their cheeks and might come out of their mouth any moment. The solid-fool (niret́-múrkha) is one who is stock full of stupidity with no room to spare. Some people think that the elephant is a large creature but its intelligence is not comparable to its large body. That is why they call some fools hastimúrkha [fools like elephants] when their intelligence is not commensurate with their size. However this expression is not wholly correct. Certain species of elephant have lower intelligence, but not all of them are unintelligent. In fact, some have sharp intelligence. Although the elephants are descendants of ancient mammoths or aerávat, still they cannot be classified into one species at present. The African elephants are quite tall but their heads are comparatively smaller; they have less intelligence and are not amenable to human control.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The branch of elephants of the indica group is smaller than African elephants, but their heads are larger. They may lack somewhat in sharpness, but they do have more or less an average intelligence. This species of elephant is found in most parts of India. Starting from West Bengal, Assam, Bhutan, and Nepal to southern Kerala are the habitats of this elephant species. They also reside in Bankura and Purulia districts of West Bengal and in Orissa. They are found in Betla sanctuary of Palamau [Jharkhand], and also reside in the Tekkari sanctuary of Kerala. At one time this elephant species was found in abundance in Karnataka; even today they are prevalent.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Another Indian elephant species of smaller size and of semi-gray colour is found in northern Assam, Cachar, Manipur and Tripura. They are of very sharp intelligence and are not easily amenable to human control. At one time they used to roam about in hordes in the forests of Tripura. They are not the elephants that we describe as domesticated elephants.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The third species of Indian elephant comprises the white elephants. In reality there is no such thing as a white elephant. Among the gray (ash) coloured elephants, there is a particular group of elephants whose colour is a shade whitish. They are also very limited in number. They are valued and respected as very sacred animals.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Bearing this in mind, would it be wise to describe someone as hastimúrkha? All animals have less intelligence than human beings. So people with lower intelligence are often described as animals. That is why some people with less intelligence are also called go-múrkha [as stupid as a cow]. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Some people think that the sour wood apple (kaed-bel) is a non-Indian fruit, imported from overseas. No, this is not correct. It is a local fruit belonging to a number of Southeast Asian countries. Its Latin name is Feronia elephantium or Feronia elephantinum. Some people might think, “Why is the name of an elephant associated with the fruit called kaed-bel or sour wood apple?” The general consensus of the people of Southeast Asia is that this is a favorite fruit of elephants. Elephants eat this fruit intact, and when the entire fruit comes out in its excreta, one can observe that the elephant has digested the entire core of the fruit, while from the outside it appears that the fruit is intact. That is why the object that appears outwardly intact but is inwardly hollow is called in Sanskrit Gajabhukta kapitthaka [like the hollow wood apple eaten by the elephant]. Elephants eat these fruit intact. They think that the whole fruit tastes very delicious. Elephants do not have the intelligence to realize that taste lies in the taste buds of the tongue; once the food goes past the tongue, there is no difference between sweetmeats and cow dung. In comparison to their size, elephants have low intelligence.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: You may be aware of the fact that among different species of elephants, the largest are the African elephants. They have a comparatively smaller head, with shorter cranium, less intelligence, and are not amenable to human control. The large Indian elephants, although physically smaller than African elephants, have a larger cranium and greater intelligence. Once, in South Asia and Tripura, the thousands of elephants that roamed about were smaller in appearance but had greater intelligence. These ash-coloured elephants sometimes vied with human beings as regards their intelligence. Out of fear of these elephants, it was impossible for trains to run at night in these regions [of Assam].
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Apart from this, in Burma and Shyámdesh (now called Thailand; the prince of Ráŕh, Sahasraváhu called this land Shyámdesh, since the country was a lush, deep green) there were white elephants (in reality, of whitish ash-colour) with average intelligence. Nevertheless, while elephants are physically large in appearance, in intelligence and sharpness they are not so great, although they cannot be described as stupid animals. ( 5 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Herd instinct of the elephant: Like the human being, the lion, the crow and other kinds of birds and beasts, the elephant also has a strong herd instinct. If the herd does not have an unquestioned leader, it breaks up in internal feuds and its security is affected. Hence you can see that when a crow is killed by someone or meets an unnatural death, thousands of crows gather together and raise their voices vociferously in their own language to protest against such an atrocity. At that time, even the most valiant retreat to safety. Those who are against hero worship in human society or are against showing respect to leadership, those who oppose individual superiority, should understand that if such individual recognition is accorded to an honest personality, it helps to guarantee the longevity of human society. If that recognition is misplaced, it becomes harmful. Human beings have advanced in knowledge, science and learning. Since by nature human beings are collective-living creatures, they must find out, irrespective of time and place, a true universal leader who should be given full recognition in the greater interest of collective welfare. Otherwise for the ever-feuding human society, there is no scope for optimism.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Yes, I was saying that elephants are herd animals. In every herd of elephants there is a leader. All other male and female elephants and their babies accept the leader without question. When this elephant leader becomes too old, physically incapable or sick, another young or capable one is chosen in its place and is given responsibility, and the old leader goes away to a lonely place.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: From the Cretaceous to the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene periods, mammoths were among the great animals that appeared on earth, and were the predecessors of elephants. Leaving aside those belonging to the reptilian class, all these large animals were herd creatures. They had similarity or uniformity in one respect: their old and physically incapacitated leader used to leave the herd and go to a secluded place, very much like people of ancient times when they became superannuated. In their extreme old age, those ancient people used to leave the society and go into váńaprastha [seclusion]. Living in the forest, they would devote themselves to worship, meditation, and to writing books. They no longer had direct social commitments.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: At the very end of old age, when they became physically incapacitated, they turned into Bhikśus [renunciates]. They had no further social obligations or mundane responsibilities. They had nothing to do except to worship the Lord in seclusion. Those who lived in isolation in forests (váńaprastha) looked after these Bhikśus. The society directly cooperated with and helped these váńaprasthiis living in the forests, and indirectly helped those who had become Bhikśus.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The malady of elephant insanity: You may have heard that sometimes elephants, particularly males, begin to lose their minds. When their heads become too heated – and especially if their tusks become too long and reach [and rub] the ground – the elephants become mad. In normal conditions, elephants never cause any harm to human beings. Wild elephants sometimes enter human settlements in search of ripe paddy or maize. Usually they come along with their families. At that time they generally remain calm. However, when they face any direct physical resistance during the collection of their food, they react and resist. Villagers often light fires in their cornfields to drive away the elephants. Elephants will then run away; they will not attack the villagers. At least, this is the experience of the villagers of Ráŕh. They do not ill-treat the elephants that are in search of ripe crops, and they do not receive any ill treatment from the elephants. I have seen simple villagers in western Ráŕh making obeisance to elephants with folded hands and praying to them.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: However, when the male elephant becomes mad, it is no longer calm and controlled. Whosoever crosses its path will be grabbed by its trunk, thrown to the ground and trampled. Occasionally in this excited state, the veins on its face burst, and lymph exudes. When this lymph is seen, one can understand that the elephant has gone mad. When it reaches such a state, it never returns to normalcy. Veterinary physicians should investigate this condition and see how they can save the elephants from this disease. ( 6 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: People once believed that if water fell from the star Sváti [the fifteenth of the twenty-seven zodiacal stars], pearls would be produced. Similarly, there was a belief that during the dark fortnight of the moon, if water fell from the Sváti star onto the head of an elephant, jewels (gajamáńikya or gajamoti or maoktika) would form on its head. When this jewel is produced, the elephants turn mad and finally die. In reality, this elephant jewel or gajamoti is something else. Compared to other animals, elephants develop more tumors (arbud) on their head. If any one of these tumors grows too large, the elephant becomes mad and eventually dies. These tumors sometimes become so hard that they cannot be broken or sliced. The common people call it gajamoti or elephant jewel. In English a shrub-like tamarisk is called Thuja, which in Sanskrit is called arbudágni. This shrub-like Thuja neutralizes the tumor. From the Sanskrit word arbud has come the Bengali word áb.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Thuja is an effective medicine in the treatment of tumors. If elephants are fed the leaves of shrubs like tamarisk on any night during the dark lunar fortnight in the month of Fálgun, Caetra or Vaeshákh [the last two months and first month of the Bengali calendar], they can be cured of this mental malady. Hence you should understand what this term gajamoti means. Whether it be from the growth of a tumor that impairs the brain of the elephant, or whether it be from the rupturing of its [facial] veins due to the scorching heat of the sun, this state of madness is known as gajamoti. And the oozing from the ruptured veins is called gajadána. ( 7 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Ivory work: In ancient times, people thought that the diamond was the hardest substance on earth and that the elephant tusk was the next hardest. People of those days had the impression that diamonds and elephant tusks could not be broken; they were to be cut with a small hand saw. As ivory and diamond craftsmanship developed, it became necessary to cut both the diamond and elephant tusk. The need for cutting diamonds arose because diamond pieces of different sizes had to be fitted into various settings while making bejeweled ornaments, especially finger rings. The diamond had to be cut according to the size required by the setting. Thus diamond-studded jewelry and diamond-studded rings came into being.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The brilliance of the diamond depends upon the skill in the cutting. Due to this technique, if even a small amount of light shines on a piece of diamond, it is reflected in myriad directions and illuminates the surroundings. Diamond glitters in shimmering light or even in near darkness solely due to the quality of its cutting. In this respect, the jewellers of the Netherlands (formerly Holland, with its capital in The Hague, and presently known as the Netherlands with its capital in Amsterdam) has earned the highest renown in terms of diamond cutting proficiency. There was a time when jewelry traders used to have costly pieces of diamond cut in Holland. Nowadays diamond cutting industries of reasonable quality have arisen in almost all countries of the world. In India the diamond craft was first developed in Mumbai. The people living in the region between Howrah and Amta, especially those living in areas adjacent to Makardaha, attained excellence as diamond craftsmen. They are now the famous diamond artisans in the market of Mumbai.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Cutting the elephant tusk is also a job requiring expertise and experience. At one time, the artisans of Bankura district developed expertise in this craft. Generally those who preoccupied themselves with terracotta art had relatives or friends who were engaged in this art. In different regions of Ráŕh, in Birbhum, Dumka, Manbhum and Singbhum districts, where there is terracotta artwork on the temples, most of the artisans who created these hailed from Bankura district. In the beginning, when the ivory craftsmen from Bankura district, Murshidabad and Dacca district won celebrity and recognition, those artists were mostly from Bankura. The ivory work of Dacca is no more. I have not inquired about the artists of Bankura. But if we made inquiries about the limited number of artists still living in Murshidabad, we could ascertain whether their predecessors belonged to Bankura. Although the art of ivory craftsmanship became popular during the middle of the Moghul period, it is a very ancient art. During the Buddhist era this craft was in vogue. The dancers of that age wore ivory rings set with diamonds.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Elephants never use their two tusks for chewing. Nowadays the tusks could be described as show pieces on the male elephants. But in ancient times, when mammoths, the ancestors of elephants, roamed on earth, their tusks were often used as weapons rather than ornaments. They used their tusks to pierce through the stomach of enemies and to level the ground in order to make a comfortable resting place. With the help of their tusks they would dig up the earth and gather it so as to create comfortable cushions for themselves.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Human beings had probably not appeared on the earth at that time. Even if humans had existed, they would have been less intelligent. Initially, they did not make use of ivory for their own benefit. When they did discover its utility, they saw that it was not only decorative but also very hard and durable. Thus they utilized it to manufacture various kinds of ornaments and merchandise. When it became a manufactured product, it became known as “ivory” instead of “tusk”. In Bengali, of course, the use of the word gajadanta continued. During the Moghul period, ivory craftsmanship enjoyed the patronage of Nawabs, their peers and lords, and the leading zamindars. ( 8 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The circle of elephant guards (Gajamańd́aliká): I have several times mentioned earlier that, like humans, elephants are social animals (they have herd instinct). The greatest enemy of the elephant is the lion. The elephant prefers dense forest. It does not bother so much about whether the place is dry or wet; but it must make sure that the water of that area is not salty and that it is deep enough. The elephant is not concerned about whether it is plains or hills; but it does require a watershed nearby because the elephant habitually bathes in water and plays in it for a good while.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Elephants are only fond of those fruits that are intoxicating or contribute to intoxication. After eating these fruits, the elephants, in an intoxicated state, plunge into the water and remain there for quite some time. There are some red berries in Africa which are very sweet and from which sugar can be produced. Elephants are very fond of these berries. If these berries are taken in large quantity (say about five or six kilos), they produce intoxication. They may not lead to intoxication in humans, but they will produce inebriation in elephants. Be that as it may, if the areas where elephants live are dry and full of bushes, and if some tall trees are also present, then lions will also be prevalent.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: The elephant is a very powerful creature. In physical strength the tiger cannot vie with the elephant. Yet the tiger has greater courage than the elephant. If there is a fight between the tiger and the elephant, there is a likelihood that the tiger will meet its death, of which it is quite aware. The reasons that the adult tiger does not want to disturb the adult wild boar are similar to the case of the tiger and the elephant. The lion does not have all these considerations. It simply attacks the elephant; sometimes the lion dies, and sometimes the elephant. Elephants have to move about cautiously, especially at night, wherever lions are more plentiful.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: In intelligence the elephant is inferior to the lion. In our Ananda Nagar area, there were once three different kinds of creatures – elephants, lions and tigers. Tigers became extinct there nearly fifty years ago, the Ráŕhii lions about ninety years ago, and the elephants have moved miles away into the distant forest. In the late autumn, they often come across again, sensing the smell of the ripe harvest.
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: In the lion-infested areas, elephants keep their females and young ones in an encircled area at night. The female elephants sleep peacefully with their cubs while the male elephants stand guard around them in a circle. Finding so many elephants together keeping guard on their herd, lions will not venture in that direction. This circle of elephant guards is known as gajamańd́aliká. Since the elephant has a herd instinct, it creates this circle of protection. Now you understand what gajamańd́aliká means. ( 9 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Auspicious elephants: At midnight, a sweet fragrance comes forth from the body of noble, well-developed elephants. If there is a mild breeze, this scent lingers for a long time; otherwise it remains for about an hour. Usually these elephants are mild-natured and dutiful, and their intelligence is sharp. Once they identify their enemies, they take severe steps against them. Otherwise, they are merry, large-hearted and sportive. These easily domesticated, large elephants are called gandhagaja. In ancient times, the kings used these elephants for their pleasure trips, but never on the battle field. ( 10 )
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
chapterTitle: Nature, Characteristics and Habits of Elephants

t: Rhinoceros: The rhinoceros (gańd́ar) is an animal from ancient times that is dying out but somehow still survives. Amongst the living animals on the earth today, it has the thickest and roughest skin. It is called gańd́ar because of its rough skin. This ancient creature may not be a contemporary of the dinosaur or brontosaurus, but it appeared on earth some time before the Pliocene Age. The rhinoceros of ancient times was very large in shape and appearance, and had two horns. Due to its horns, it is also called shruṋgiká [horned creature]. You would know better that our familiar, two-horned scaleless fish (siuṋgi mách) has a better name, shruṋgiká. (The other name of mágur or catfish is mudgara fish.) Among those known as shruṋgiká, the rhinoceros is the largest.

At one time the northern and eastern regions of India, which are mostly rainswept, provided a habitat for the rhinoceros. In most parts of Bengal the rhinoceros used to move about, if not in hundreds of thousands, then at least in the thousands. In ancient times there might have been various rhinoceros species; but today it is confined to three species; the one-horned rhino, the two-horned rhino and the small-sized rhino. The one-horned rhino and two-horned rhino dwelt in Assam, North Bengal and the Terai areas of Nepal (in Madhya Desh or Madesh); even today some of them can be seen there. In the Dooars (Himalayan foothills) areas of Jalpaiguri, when humans had not yet settled down, a huge number of rhinos were found, especially in the Hashimara region.

The maximum number of rhinoceros was found in Jalpaiguri. Aside from this, one could find them in northeast Rangpur and in Rangpur. Of course, in the Nilfamari region of Rangpur district [now in Bangladesh], about 125 years ago there were plenty of rhinos – both the single-horned and double-horned varieties. Not only in North Bengal, in the Sahebganj district of Rárh, in Birbhum district, and in the Rajmahal hills of Dumka district, in the dense jungle of sábui grass about 150 years ago, herds of rhinoceros used to roam. Along with the rhinos, numerous large pythons and countless myna birds abounded.

Where have those rhinos, big pythons and mynas gone? People must have killed the pythons and used their fat to adulterate clarified butter. Relentlessly trapping the mynas and putting them in cages, people have thwarted their breeding and growth.
