The wool of the yaks is lengthy and handsome. Many a time the attractive appearance of a human being or an animal winds up being the cause of that creatureʼs death. The impressive hide of the deer or its horns is often responsible for its death; the wings of the bright green insect are often responsible for its death; once the feathers of a peacock were considered to be the cause of its death. Similarly, the handsome hair of the camrii is often considered to be the cause of its death. It is said: Kesheśu camriiḿ hanti, meaning, “for its hair a yak is killed”.

In English camrii is called yak. The female yak is called giripriyá. Some people firmly believe that the ox on which Lord Shiva used to roam around the world was no ordinary ox, but a male yak. Apparently the male yak is somewhat ferocious looking. At least, people of the plains would become frightened at its initial appearance, although there is no reason to fear it. It is very calm and quiet by nature. On its own it never attacks anyone; and even when attacked, it does not normally retaliate. It fights only when its life is in danger. Its lengthy, beautiful hair, when tied around a stick, is known as cámar. In ancient times, ritually blessed persons used to be fanned with a cámar.

Usually, on reaching the five different stages of life, one had to pass through certain rituals called abhiśek. The first was at the early stage of childhood on the occasion of játakarma or naming ceremony; the second was during the sacred thread ceremony; the third was the marriage ceremony; the fourth was upon ascension to the throne or when being crowned as the crown prince; and the fifth was when, by the grace of the Guru, one received initiation into higher spiritual practices. This kind of spiritual initiation at the directive of the Guru was called Sámrájya Diikśá [initiation of universal sovereignty]. On this occasion, at the directive of the Guru, one of his junior disciples used to fan his senior disciple with the cámar. These five stages combined were called Paiṋcábhiśek [five-fold initiation]. On these occasions, there was the practice of using conch shells, five lamps and the cámar. Yes, Kesheśu cámriiḿ hanti – for the sake of its hair, the yak was killed by humans. ( 9 )

Dwindling usefulness of our domestic animals: You all know that in everyday life people are reducing the use of animals. The job of tilling is now being done by power-tillers and tractors. The bullock cart is going out of use; the use of the horse-carriage is now as good as nil. For the sake of milk, people will probably keep cows for some time to come. After the discovery of synthetic milk, people will give up keeping cows at home, since for tilling and milking cows will no longer be necessary. For use in oil mills, bullocks have already become redundant.

Just as the necessity of cows will disappear in future, the necessity of horses also has almost come to an end. I surmise that in some dayʼs time, the horse will turn into an animal in the zoo. However, there was a time when the word ‘carriage’ was inalienably linked up with the horse, and along with the carriage they would invariably use the expression ‘horse-carriage’ (ghoŕá-gáŕii). In the field of speed, the horse was in such high demand! In the past, on the roads and resting places, on highways, in big towns and at road crossings, there was an arrangement for keeping large cisterns for quenching the thirst of horses and for bathing them by the roadside. In our own city of Kolkata, at various places there were such big cisterns filled with water. The black gram that was kept as fodder for the horses was soaked in these cisterns. In the Buddhist and even post-Buddhist eras, such large cisterns filled with water were prevalent on the roads and city thoroughfares. ( 10 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Dog family and cat family: You all know that our familiar carnivorous animals are divided into two families: the cat and the dog families. Animals belonging to the cat family have round faces with whiskers (even the tigress and the female cat have whiskers). They are not at all inclined to live as a family. They have sharp intelligence and courage, but they display their courage by applying intelligence; that is, they do not like to endanger themselves by simply making a show of their courage. Animals belonging to the cat family have little tolerance towards other animals. Animals belonging to the dog family (in Sanskrit kukkura or kukura; in Bengali kukur) have long and pointed faces; some of them even live in families (such as the lion). They have average intelligence. They thrust themselves into dangerous situations to display their courage. They are quite generous in nature and even make sacrifices.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: In the dog family, the largest animal is the African lion, now on the verge of extinction. The lions of Ráŕh became extinct about one hundred years ago. The Gujrat lion, the lion of Girnar or the Gir lion, both male and female, have no mane. In another lion species, only the males have a mane and not the females. (In Sanskrit and Bengali a lion is called siḿha, in Persian babar, in English lion, in Latin leo). Apart from this, there is the wolf in northern India called lákŕá bágh (in Sanskrit called brka, in English known as wolf). Then there are different species of dogs and jackals. Amongst these familiar animals, the smallest is the fox.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Among the feline species the largest of them all is the kudo bágh or Royal Bengal Tiger of the Sundarbans. In Bengali it is called bágh, in Sanskrit byághra or shárdul, in Persian sher and in English tiger. There are black tigers, then jaguars of South America, gulbághás or panthers, cheetahs, and chitra byághras or leopards. Then there are also hyenas, which are called huŕárs, huńd́árs, begoyás, gobághás, in Sanskrit tarakśu. Smaller than this is the civet cat (bhám), the pole cat (khat́t́ásh, in spoken Bengali kát́t́ash), wild cats and our own domesticated cat.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Both animals of the cat and dog families are carnivorous; they do not eat uncooked vegetarian food, although they sometimes eat cooked food. What is interesting is that although there are large and small varieties of dogs, they are not of any distinct subspecies. Its father is a wolf and its mother is a female jackal. Such is the identity of the dog. That is why, while seeking primitive fossils, I have come across the fossils of wolves and the fossils of jackals, but no fossils of the dog. In their early stage, all animals belonging to the dog family look very much alike. As they grow up, differences in their appearance become prominent; their cry also becomes distinct from other animals. Alsatians are very close to wolves. Domesticated wolves (they are not easily amenable to human control) and Alsatians have very little differences. They have a very powerful sense of smell and can easily differentiate between various kinds of scents. Hence in the task of apprehending criminals, they help human beings to a great extent. Both the dog and cat families of animals make distinctive sounds. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The dog is a sharp-snouted member of the canine family, and the tiger is a round-snouted member of the feline family. There is an inherent hostility between these two. According to biologists, members of the canine family are sharp-snouted, carnivorous, swift runners, make noise when they run, and have a strong sense of smell (the Alsatian is an exception). They also display a great deal of affection towards their young. The largest animal in this group is the maned lion, native to Africa. In addition, there is the medium-sized, maned Indian lion, the maneless Indian lion or gurjar lion, the wolf (brkabyághra), Alsatian, ( 2 ) the ordinary domesticated Indian dog, the wild Indian dog, the jackal (shrgála), the fox (ulkámukhii), and so on. In addition there are many kinds of short-haired and long-haired dogs differing in variety and from country to country. Some people are of the opinion that while the dog no doubt belongs to the canine family, it is not an original species but rather a cross-breed – the wolf is its father and the jackal its mother; this was the ancient conception.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Although dogs live in groups, different members of the canine family do not mix with each other. For example, wolves and lions are not on good terms with each other. Wolves will chase a dog if they see one and will kill it, regardless of whether they eat it or not. Dogs will also chase jackals if they see them.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The tiger, however, is a different family of animal, a feline. Members of the feline family do not remain in groups. They are extremely greedy and self-seeking. The father does not show one iota of affection towards his progeny and often kills them. Members of this family suffer great pain at the time of dying. Even though the father does not feel any affection for his progeny, the mother does to a great extent. Female cats and tigers raise their young with a great deal of affection and even cry for a long time when their offspring die. ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The fundamental difference between the cat family and the dog family is that animals of the dog family move around in search of prey, just as the dog moves in search of food. It sniffs here and there, and, if not getting the desired object, runs somewhere else. Creatures of the cat family do not do this; at a convenient place they wait and come upon a scent and then, following the scent, suddenly swoop down upon their prey. Of course tigers also jump or leap upon their prey; that is why the tiger that leaps upon its prey is called ‘leaping tiger’. In the smaller arena, the cat also leaps upon the rat in a similar manner.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Creatures of the dog family always leave an impression of sincerity in all their activities. By proving their manliness, they satisfy their ego. Even risking their life, they nourish their manliness. Animals of the cat family do not do so. They are opportunists; seeking an opportunity, they act. This is the difference between the cat and the dog.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: That also is the distinction between the lion and the tiger. The lion, due to its imperial appearance and its mane, is called the king of animals, although its physical strength is less than that of the Royal Bengal Tiger. Like other creatures of the dog family, the intelligence of the lion is somewhat less than that of the tiger. The lion and other members of the dog family act rashly and without premeditation. Animals of the cat family never do this. The creatures of the dog family often live in herds and in families. Those of the cat family never do so.They believe in exclusiveness and solitary life. They have no friends, no allies, none with whom to share their pleasures and woes, to whom they can communicate their feelings. They are entirely solitary.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Since the animals of the dog family have less intelligence, they often retreat in their battle for life; even the members of the cat family are also losing the battle for existence, but to a far less extent than members of the dog family. The African lion – the powerful and gigantic king of maned animals – is very large in size. The females do not have manes. At one time lions were the undisputed monarchs in the African savannah. No one dared to do battle with them for power. It was as if the lion felt: “I am the monarch of all I survey; no one dare to dispute my sovereign rights.” Even then, lions lost the battle of intelligence to frail creatures – human beings. The Sahara Desert and the large stretch of forestland to the south no longer reverberate with the triumphant roar of the lion. Yes, there are lions; but theirs is not real living, it is just survival. Even in our Ráŕh region, the heavily forested sandy beds of the Mayurákśii, Ajay, Damodar, Dvarakeshvar and Subarnarekha rivers once reverberated with the roars of lions.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Although the Ráŕhii lion was smaller in size than the African lion, the appearance of the males was impressive. Compared to its body, the face was quite large, and the teeth sharper. It is about 150 years since Dumka, Birbhum and Samantabhum became devoid of lions. Other areas –Sikharbhum, Senbhum, Manbhum, Bhanjabhum, Singhabhum, Barahabhum, and Sabarbhum – are also now bereft of lions. Even a century ago the females of this species had no manes. Yet in their sweeping forcefulness, in their raging violence, in their vanity of existence, they were simply unrivaled. Due to their uncongenial environment on the red soil of Ráŕh, these lions have become extinct. Only some fossils of this animal are found on the riverbeds of the dying and narrow rivers. The Girnar lion of western India, although unsightly in appearance, somehow survived in the hilly forest areas of Girnar in Gujrat due to its more congenial environment. As a result of recent conservation measures, the Girnar lion has been partially preserved [from extinction]. Still homelier than this unsightly lion, the females of this species are more numerous today because of their superior intelligence. If governmental safeguards are withdrawn at any time, it will not be long before these lions become extinct. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Nature and habitat of the lion: The lion (siḿha) is a long-faced animal belonging to the dog family (the tiger belongs to the round-faced feline family.) [As mentioned earlier] the largest animal of this family is the African lion. Huge in appearance, with a large face, the male lions have manes. Of course, the lioness has no mane. If there are hills nearby, they live in caves; where there are no hills they live in the bush. They do not like dense forests. Another large animal of this family is the Rárhii lion. About one hundred to one hundred twenty five years ago, on the dry fields and the forests of Ráŕh, these lions used to roam about triumphantly. Their kingdoms were in Dumka, Deoghar, the southwest of Birbhum (i.e., in Dubrajpur and Khairashol areas), West Burdwan, Bankura, West Midnapur, Bhainjabhum and Manbhum (in Purulia, Dhanbad and other areas). Many villages of these areas have the word siḿha and gharghará associated with them. Near Ananda Nagar is the village Siḿghághrá (siḿhagharghárá). Close to it is Ghágrá (gharghará) village. There are many villages associated with the word siḿha, such as Birsiḿha, Banbirsiḿha, etc. Kings used to have names like SiḿhaVáhu, Vijaysingha, and so on. Some time ago, in the adjoining areas of the Shushunia hills (Bankura), the fossils of lion jaws were discovered, just as fossils of large mammoths have also been found in that region. Somewhat smaller in appearance than the Ráŕhii lion is the Girnar lion of Gujarat. The male Girnar lions do not have manes. From a distance they look somewhat like dogs. ( 5 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The large lions of Africa used to roam about in large number in the savannah and dry bushland of Africa and in the southern areas of the Sahara desert. Recently, their number has gone down appreciably. The males have manes, while the females do not.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The Girnar lions of Gujarat, or of the Girnar forest, are inhabitants of the dry, semi-desert areas of Gujarat. Their number has dwindled to such an extent that they have nearly come to the point of extinction. Due to special efforts by the Government of India to save this species, their population has increased to some extent. This is a good sign.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Once the [Rárhii lion] used to roam throughout Ráŕh, especially in western Ráŕh, in large numbers. Even today in the Shushunia hills of Bankura, in the Biharilal (some say Biharinath) hills, in Panchakot of Manbhum, Tilabani, Joichandi and Ayodhya hills, in the Dalma hills of Singhbhum, in Bhanjabhum, in Dimdiha of Manbhum, in the hills of Sapkuthi, Taherbera and Jabar hills [near Ananda Nagar], many such lion fossils can be found. This Rárhii lion became completely extinct nearly ninety years ago. [As mentioned earlier], once the favourite haunts of the Rárhii lion were the bushes of Baglata, Gurabazar and Guridi, adjacent to Ananda Nagar. Today there is not a single lion in that area. Yet the names of the villages are associated with the lion – Siḿghaghará [the roaring sound of the lion], Ghágrá [the roar of the lion], Sat́ká [the runaway lion], Bághlatá [Baglata; where the tiger cowers down]. The names of the villages bear out the intimate relations of these places with the lion. ( 6 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Wolf (brka byághra): Our very familiar animal, the wolf (lákŕá or nekŕe bágh, in Sanskrit brka byághra) belongs to the dog family. This dog-faced animal is a peculiar species of the Ráŕh region. In the conservation areas of Ráŕh, this type of wolf can be found even today in sufficient numbers. They live in the caves of hills, in rough terrain, and in hollows in the ground. As little as seventy years ago, near the police stations of Rajnagar in Birbhum, these wolves were a source of worry to the owners of domesticated animals. Today, because of deforestation, there is hardly a single wolf in Birbhum, although there are some in other districts. The proverb ‘wolf at the door’ is derived from the greedy nature of wolves. The Alsatians and various wild dogs also come in this category. It is interesting to note that these latter animals live in herds. They believe in living together as a group, unlike cats such as the civet cat, wild cat, polecat, etc. who prefer to live in isolation. ( 7 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The wolf – lákŕá or lákaŕ bághá in north India – is always going out for the purpose of eating. In some peopleʼs opinion, the wolf can take into its stomach significantly more than the weight of its own body. Just as the ant can carry a load that is much heavier than its own body, the wolf can eat more. The wolf has very little capacity for carrying loads. Due to his excessive gluttony, the second Pandava brother, Bhima, used to be called Brkodara (one whose stomach is like a wolfʼs). During the time that the Pandavas were incognito, mother Kunti would take the food they would bring home from begging and give half of it to Bhima. The remainder she and her other four sons would eat.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Ardha khán Kuntii saha cári sahodare,
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Ardhek báṋt́iyá den viirbrkodare.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: [Half the four brothers eat along with Kunti, half is apportioned to the brave Bhima.] ( 8 )]
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Alsatian: You are all familiar with the Alsatian. We look upon the Alsatian as a dog, but in reality it is not a dog. It is an animal very close to the wolf family. Of course, there is a fundamental difference between the two. There are four factors that separate them from each other. The first point of difference is that although the wolf has a very strong sense of smell, the Alsatian has an even stronger sense of smell.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The second point of difference is that the wolf, whether it eats it or not, will slay a dog that crosses its path. But the wild Alsatian (let alone the domesticated Alsatian) is not that hostile towards the dog.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The third point of difference is that the wolf can consume food about two and half times its own size. After that, of course, it lies flat on the ground for a few days like a dead animal. The Alsatian does not eat so much.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Fourthly, the wolf is not easily amenable to domestication, but the Alsatian can be domesticated and is very devoted to its master. In ancient times the crossbreeding of the wolf and the jackal led to the birth of the dog. There is no proof actually as to whether the wolf and the jackal, in the same manner, crossbred to produce the Alsatian. If at all there is a mixture of the wolf and the jackal in the Alsatian, there is more of the wolf.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: In all languages of the world, there is mention of the wolf but not the Alsatian. In Sanskrit the wolf is called brk byághra. In the Vedic age there were vague references to the fact that some human beings, after killing the wolf, used to eat its meat, particularly its heart. In Sanskrit literature, even in ancient Bengali literature, there are references to the wolf as a voracious eater. ( 9 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Jackal: The jackal (shiyál) is a very familiar animal of the equatorial region. Its history is also very old. This animal reached its present state through several evolutions. People of various countries of the world have ruthlessly slaughtered jackals due to their greed for wool and leather. There are even some tribals in India who eat the meat of jackals.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Synonyms of shiyál are shivá, yambuka, jambukukkura, badrikukkura, etc. Berries are a favourite fruit of jackals. That is why jackals are called jambukukkura and badrikukkura. Jackals are eaten by tribal people. Apart from this, there is a small group of people in Ráŕh who are known as shiálkhore [jackal-eaters] or shiálkhego [jackal-eating people]. Although jackals like jujube fruits, they are also very fond of berries. ( 10 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Fox: The fox (khekshiyál) makes the khi… khi… khi sound more often than it scowls or snarls. Hence the khi… khi sound indicates a fox and not a jackal. Of course, the chaste Sanskrit word for fox is ulkámukhii. Some people believe that foxes have phosphorus in their mouth and teeth, and as they scowl, due to contact with the air, that phosphorus lights up. The Sanskrit word ulká means meteor in English. Because its mouth glitters, it is called ulkámukhii in Sanskrit.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: In North India khikir means fox. One does not have to search for foxes in the forest. Wherever there are jujube trees (plum trees), one will find these animals in their vicinity in holes in the ground. Both the jackal and the fox belong to the same family. In ancient times they had the same ancestors. Nowadays the fox is smaller in size than the jackal. The protruding part of their mouth is somewhat different. Both are nocturnal creatures. Of course, the fox more than the jackal sometimes emerges during the daytime. When the fox yawns, its mouth lights up, but this is not so with the jackal. The skin of the fox is thinner than the skin of the jackal, so nothing can be made from the skin of the fox; but yarns, shoes and caps are prepared from the hide of the jackal. Few people are interested in eating foxes. It is said that the meat of the fox is very hard and dry. In the spring, winter and summer, fox droppings are full of jujube seeds. One can thus easily find out the habits of foxes. The cry of the fox sounds like khi- khi- khi- khi and that of the jackal sounds like hukká-huá, hukká-huá. At night jackals cry out together in herds, but foxes do not do so. ( 11 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Dog: The word kukkura [dog] is also used in the sense of kukura. The word kukkura is formed by adding the suffix urań to the verbal root kuk. In it there is an additional ka. Some call the suffix kurańa as well. The word kukur is prevalent both in Bengali and in Bhojpuri. The word is used in its original Sanskrit form. In Punjabi it is called kukkur. The word is derived from Sanskrit. Again, according to some, the original Sanskrit word is kukkura, and kukura is the prákrta form [spoken form] or the grhita Sanskrit form [word from another language accepted in Sanskrit].
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: According to some zoologists, a dog is not an original species [sui generis]; it is a hybrid creature. According to some scholars, a dog is a hybrid of the wolf and the vixen. In ancient times wild dogs were rather scarce, precisely for the same reason. There is hardly any dog fossil amongst the available fossils of ancient animals. Nowadays, however, wild dogs are also prevalent. These wild dogs live gregariously in jungles, and even a gigantic tiger has been seen to be flabbergasted and killed by a concerted attack of these dogs.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Although the dog is a hybrid of the wolf and the vixen, it must be said that there are many radical, extreme differences between a wolf and a dog. A wolf is voracious, but a dog feels satisfied with a small meal. It is difficult to tame a wolf, but a dog loves to be domesticated. A dog is extremely faithful and loyal to its master. A wolf is neither faithful nor loyal to its master. A dog is not ferocious by nature. It attacks or frightens someone as part of its duty. A wolf is ferocious by nature. It has no sense of duty. A dog would not normally kill a creature if its stomach were full. But a wolf, even when its belly is full, kills a creature. If it has no capacity to eat, it carries the carcass to its den and eats it according to its convenience. Dogs do not generally fight with other members of the dog family. They fight with members of the feline family. But a wolf does not observe any such principle. A wolf avoids the strong and unnecessarily attacks the weak. Although there is a family resemblance between the wolf and the dog, whenever a dog is sighted the wolf attacks and kills it.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: There are many differences between a jackal and a dog. A dog generally moves about during the daytime, but jackals are night prowlers by nature. A jackal moves in the daytime only when it is in danger, it has to change location or is excessively hungry. A jackal lives in a hole, but a dog never likes to live in a hole. It prefers to live in the open. A jackal cannot be tamed; but a dog can. By virtue of being night prowlers, jackals periodically howl in chorus to preserve their solidarity and register their presence. However, dogs do not have this habit. They bark collectively only when they have to fight an enemy as a body. Although both jackals and dogs belong to the canine family, a dog chases a jackal whenever it sees one. A jackal runs away at the sight of a dog. By nature a dog is brave and a jackal is cowardly.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The Alsatian dogs are close relatives of foxes. The dogs of Bhutan, although not cowardly, closely resemble jackals in cold countries.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Although a fox belongs to the dog family, its relation with the dog is very remote. In spite of some similarity between a dog and a jackal in appearance, there is a wide gulf of difference in their natures.
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: The dog has been a companion of human beings since ancient times. History tells us that dogs have been of use and continue to be of use to people in different ways, in their prosperity as well as in their adversity. In the scriptures, a dog has sometimes been shown respect by presenting it as a symbol of dharma. Of course, there is no dearth of people who are opposed to dogs. In northern India, some people say: “Only one who is a dog himself maintains a dog.” In Hindi and Urdu, kukura [dog] is called kuttá. ( 12 )
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
chapterTitle: Lions and Other Dog Family Members

t: Tiger: The second meaning of the word khat́akhádaka is byághra or tiger (bi-á-ghra + d́a = byághra); that is, a creature whose olfactory organ is very strong. If a tiger senses the specific scent of its prey, it will easily locate it and then rush out to seize it. Just as the crow is khat́akhádaka by virtue of its lips, similarly a tiger is khat́akhádaka by virtue of its nails and teeth. Another characteristic of the tiger is that by mere conjecture [instinct] it can take a precise leap and fall exactly upon its prey.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: There are various types of tigers in the world. Of course, chief among them are the Royal Bengal tiger, black tiger, panther, cheetah (leopard), hyena, civet cat or pole cat, wild cat and our domesticated cat (not wolves, because they belong to the dog family).
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: There are many similarities and dissimilarities between tigers and lions – both carnivorous animals. Judging from circumstances, the tiger must have come to India from the direction of China, while the lion must have been the original inhabitant of India. The tiger loves rain-affected regions and dense forest areas. It even likes slightly salty water. The lion is fond of land with scanty rainfall and bushy forests. It does not like salty water. Both tigers and lions are courageous animals. In physical strength, the Royal Bengal tigers of the Sundarbans are far more powerful than the African or Ráŕh lions. The lions of Gujarat are more powerful than certain types of tigers and weaker than others. Whether weak or powerful, all lions are courageous, and all tigers are valiant. Both tigers and lions have qualitative distinctiveness. Both are good looking. The tiger is much more intelligent than the lion. If tigers moving in the forest notice that some tree branches have been chopped off, they will suspect that enemies are lurking nearby. If it finds that a goat has been kept tied up in a secluded spot in the forest, it might feel tempted to attack, but it will not go forward and fall upon its prey immediately. Glancing all around, it will advance surreptitiously and run away with the goat. It runs away so fast that even the hunters are stunned. However, the lion has somewhat of a devil-may-care disposition: “Let the enemy come, I donʼt care; surely no one can beat me in physical strength,” is how the lion feels. Without looking around, and even risking its own life, it will fall upon its prey – the goat. It is not as greedy as the tiger or the wolf, especially when its stomach is full. It does not normally attack anyone without reason but it will counterattack someone who charges first. Compared to the tiger, the lion is more compassionate. Not only for its own progeny – which even the tiger feels – it has been found to have affection even for the offspring of other animals. Evidence of this behaviour has been documented.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: The damp areas of the Sundarbans are very congenial for tigers, but not for lions. The lion can hardly endure the salty water of that area. While the dry climate and sweet water of Ráŕh are quite congenial for lions, they are not at all congenial for the tiger. Hence in ancient times, although tigers were primarily concentrated in Bengal, both tigers and lions lived in Ráŕh. That is why the Puranic gods and goddesses have both tigers and lions as their mounts; the mount of the tiger god of the forest (Dakśiń Ráy) is naturally a tiger, and the mount for the goddess Rájrájershvarii is a tiger on the back of an elephant. Meanwhile, the mount of the Puranic goddess Durgá is a lion.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: The tiger, having a round face, is an animal of the cat family. Animals of both the dog family and the cat family have a very powerful sense of smell. However, animals of the dog family have to concentrate in order to track a scent. To understand where the milk or fish or meat is, the dog has to apply its mind, and only then does it pick up the scent; but animals of the cat family spontaneously get the scent through their nose. The cat does not have to apply any special faculty to know where in the house the milk or fish is located. The scent wafts towards it, and the cat is compelled by natural law to run in that direction. If the housekeeper drives it away, even then the cat remains drawn by the scent, voluntarily or involuntarily. We say that even after a beating, the cat forgets after some time and returns. Whether the cat received a beating or not, it is a particular scent that draws it back. Among the animals of the cat family, the tiger also has a very powerful sense of smell. The derivative meaning of the word byághra is “one who has a very strong sense of smell”. The number of tiger species is quite large. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Pole cat: Khat́t́ash or kat́t́ásh is a feline animal. The derivative meaning of the word khat́t́ásh is “one which rests on a soft bed or prefers a soft bed”. In common usage, khat́t́ásh means “creatures of the cat family”.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: You all know that animals of the cat family love a comfortable environment. They prefer a soft bed or the cozy side of an oven. The pole cat (khat́t́ásh) is an animal that lives outside the house; but even in the forests or bushes it prefers to lie down on soft grass or on soft creepers and the leaves of a tree. Although by nature they are not timid, they are afraid of humans. So they prefer to live apart from human settlements.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: After construction of the dam on the Damodar River, in Ráŕh and in South Bengal the Jalangi, Mathabhanga, Ichamati, Kumar, Bhaerava, Nabaganga, Garai, Madhumati, Shivsa, Rupsa and Citra Rivers all dried up. As a result there was a severe onslaught of malaria in the region. Once known for its wealth and clamour of human beings, once resounding with the notes of birds, the then Banagram of Jessore district turned into a forest, having fallen victim to all-engulfing malaria. Due to fear of malaria, many people left their hearth and home and settled in and around Kolkata on the bank of the Bhagirathi. Not only Banagram, but three other sub-divisions r– Magura, Jessore-Sadar and Jhinaidaha – were reduced to the same plight, except for the Narail sub-division of Jessore. People moved away, and in their place came pole cats or Kat́t́ásh, herds of them. So there was a popular saying: “Kat́t́ásh is the king of Banagram and the lion of the forest.” ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Civet cat (gandhagokul): The gokul [cat] that emits a sweet smell [gandha] is called gandhagokul [civetcat]. You know that certain creatures possess certain kinds of smell, good or bad. This is nothing but the secretion of hormones from certain glands. The glandular secretions of the musk rat emit a bad smell. While moving, the musk rat emits a foul smell particularly from the secretion of its lymphatic glands, which distresses the human nose. Due to differences in their hormones, the pungent smell that emanates from a tigerʼs body does not exude from the body of a cat. This smell can be perceived to a very small degree from the body of a wildcat (ban-beŕál). You will scarcely notice this in a khat́t́ásh (or kat́ash). Yet you would notice an odour in a similar but comparatively smaller creature such as the bhám. Though smaller than tigers, hyenas have this bad smell about them. Certain animals with testicles emit a foul smell from the secretion of their glands, but not when their testicles are removed. So the good or bad smell indicates the smell derived from the glandular secretion of hormones. Male goats with testicles have a severe foul smell; but goats without testicles have no foul odour at all. People who consume too much of onions, garlic and meat, which are difficult to digest, emit a bad smell from the secretion of certain glands. Hence excessive intake of onions, garlic, hard-to-digest meat and certain vegetables invariably causes a bad smell in human beings.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Those who are careful about taking food and do not allow profuse sweating will not generate a bad odour from their body. Of course, sweat itself has no smell, but when it remains on the body for more than 45 minutes, a bad odour develops. The moment the bad smell starts to develop, it is advisable to mop the sweat from the body with a towel or piece of cloth, or wash it off with water. On the other hand, persons who do yogic exercises or take part in devotional singing of kiirtana continuously for a long time secrete certain hormones from specific parts of their anáhata cakra [fourth psycho-spiritual plexus], vishuddha cakra [fifth plexus] and ájiṋá cakra [sixth plexus]. Such secretions emit a sweet fragrance similar to jasmine or ripe jackfruit (although not exactly comparable). So, devotees or yogis generally have a sentient aroma. One of the signs of pure love for God is the emanation of a sweet fragrance from the body of a devotee. When a person even in seclusion tries to feel the spiritual proximity of Parama Puruśa, they can feel the presence of a sweet fragrance wafting across the nose. This is in fact nothing but the sweet-smelling hormones secreted from their glands and concentrated at the tip of the nose. Although a biological phenomenon (related to bio-psychology), it can only be looked upon as the grace of the Supreme.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: According to natural law, there are certain creatures whose bodies emanate a fragrance similar to sweet-smelling sunned rice. The gandhagokul [civet-cat] is one such creature. This creature, which is midway between the fox and the mole of the forest, can hardly see in the daylight. Like owls, they are almost blind during the day, but are not blind at night. Since they see very little during the day and are afraid of dogs, they do not come out in the daytime. At night, when they stay somewhere for any length of time, they leave behind the sweet scent of fragrant, sunned rice.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: The gandhagokul [civet-cat] is a creature of the Ráŕh region. Once they could be found in large numbers in Burdwan, Medinipur, Bankura and Manbhum districts; but because of human oppression they are about to become extinct. By nature they are timid. That is why people often slay them. If arrangements are not made to safeguard their lives, in the near future they will disappear from the face of the earth.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: By comparison, in order to save them from danger, nature has given to some helpless creatures the power to exude a foul smell through glandular secretions. The llama, which is an animal of the camel group, feels endangered when attacked by enemies and emanates a very foul smell from its body, due to the secretion of hormones from its glands. Due to that foul smell, the enemy is compelled to run away. ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: The meaning of the word otu is “one who hunts a scent”, and gandhotu means “someone who preys upon a creature by their scent”. Cats or animals of the cat family usually prey upon something or someone. So in the etymological sense, gandhotu means, “one who preys by scent” or “creatures of the cat family”. In common usage, gandhotu means bhám [the civet cat].
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: The Royal Bengal Tiger of the Sundarbans, the black tigers and jaguars of South America, the panthers and the leopards, all belong to the cat family. Of course, the original cheetahs became extinct about fifty years ago. Smaller than these cheetahs are the gobághá or hárols or bigobá, in English they are called hyenas and in Sanskrit tarakśu. These gobághá or hyenas are smaller in size than normal tigers. Hence they are afraid of adult humans. Next to them [in size] are the bháms. Smaller than bhám cats are the pole cats (khát́t́ás ) and even smaller are the wild cats (bon-beŕál), our known kuṋdo beŕál, domesticated cats (the tomcat and the female cat – meni beŕál). Beginning with the Royal Bengal Tiger up to the civet cat, they are all very similar in appearance and nature. They emit a very foul odour from their body. The kat́ás, bon-beŕál and kuṋdo-beŕáls are smaller in size. In addition, they eat food other than meat. Hence their bodies barely emit any strong odour … in fact, they have almost no smell at all. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Royal Bengal Tiger: The second meaning of the word karvara is “proud animal” or “large tiger”. Another name for what we call “Royal Bengal tiger” in English, kuṋdo bágh in Bengali, is karvara. It is the largest member of the cat family. Among its various traits are its keen intelligence and its powerful sense of smell. It is able to ascertain which animals are found in each direction by checking the wind.
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Although they are much stronger than humans, they are much less intelligent, and they know this. So if they catch a human scent in the wind, they prefer not to tread that path. However, if they happen on a person unexpectedly, they will attack them out of a sense of self-preservation. There are a small number of karvara tigers who, despite belonging to the same family, develop a taste for human flesh by eating dead bodies in burial grounds or in the forest. Some can no longer struggle with other animals in their old age, and therefore kill and eat human beings because humans cannot run from them or match them in physical strength. It is very easy for them to kill humans, so those karvara tigers who become man-eaters in this way, and remain so for a long time, undergo some physical changes. Their snout becomes comparatively long and their stomach becomes thinner. If people are aware of which Bengal tigers are man-eaters and which are not, they can take more precautionary measures. ( 5 )
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
chapterTitle: Tiger and Other Cat Family Members

t: Evolution of the ape family – tailless apes:

You all know that animals are chiefly of two types, graminivorous (feeding on grasses and cereals) and carnivorous. Graminivorous animals usually have hooves and are without paws, while carnivorous animals have paws for feet. Graminivorous animals have sparkling white teeth which are carefully arranged. Carnivorous animals have uneven teeth, slightly yellowish, or reddish yellow in colour. They have canine teeth on both sides of the mouth for tearing flesh.

Among graminivorous animals, particularly those creatures belonging to the zebu species (or bison genus) had an ability to store food in their appendix. This developed during ancient times, when they lived in a volatile situation, unsure of obtaining food at all times. Apes, humans and goats all developed this capacity. Cows and buffaloes also did, and they still do today. As life becomes more and more secure, the necessity for this appendix also diminishes. This has happened to humans, apes and certain other animals. During leisure time, by regurgitating food from the appendix, these animals make it fit for digestion with the help of saliva. In English this is called rumination or chewing the cud; in Bengali it is called románthan or jábar kát́á. Carnivorous animals do not have this capacity, because the meat they have eaten quickly decomposes and develops a foul odour. It cannot be used for rumination or for chewing the cud.

In ancient times, those land-dwelling, graminivorous animals without horns or claws for self-preservation began to climb trees in search of safe refuge. For those animals, just as the necessity for using hooves came to an end, they now felt the need for using their forelimbs to catch hold of tree branches. They used their hind legs partly for clutching and partly for running. They used their forelimbs for clutching branches of trees as well as for other tasks. In ancient times, the forelimbs were earlier called kara, and later hasta. Australopithecines, creatures of the ape family, and human beings are all equipped with kara. In fact, they have four limbs; but human beings are not quadrupeds because their forelimbs are used for clutching objects.

In order to climb trees and to leap up, the creatures of the ape family required a tail. However, for the more intelligent [members] of this family who no longer needed to leap as much, the importance of the lymphatic gland diminished and their tails dropped off. This superfamily of creatures – the apes – gradually split into two family lines. Both families had well-arranged teeth and no canine teeth. Both had an intestinal appendix, but one family had a tail and the other was tailless. Those with tails, belonging to the ape family, are called monkeys – in Bengali bánar or bádar, and the females bánarii or bádarii, in Urdu bandar, and the females bandariá. The tailless monkeys had greater intellectual development than those with tails. They also evolved into two different classes: one ordinary and the other more developed. Of the ordinary tailless apes there were again three distinct genuses; 1) gorillas, 2) orang-utans (in Malay language it means “men of the trees”) and 3) chimpanzees. Today the developed, tailless apes are known as humans. The word “man” stands for “mentally developed ape”.

This is how we differentiate the types of graminivorous animals. The human being is naturally a vegetarian creature without a developed intestinal appendix. So regular intake of meat might cause the ailment of appendicitis in humans – this does occur often. Regular intake of meat for humans is an unnatural habit which does not provide any benefit. ( 1 )

The ape family: Ku+d́ikhin = kikhi. The verbal root ku is used in many senses. One meaning is grinning and grimacing. So the etymological meaning of the word kikhi is “one who grimaces”. One speciality about the suffixes d́ikhin and kvan is that the last phoneme of the verbal root can alternately be i. For example, if you add the suffix kvan/kvas to the verbal root kan, the resulting word will of course be kańva, but it can also be kińva. Similarly, if you add the suffix d́ikhin, it can be both kukhi and kikhi. But the kukhi form is not prevalent. In common usage, the word kikhi means monkey. On the slightest occasion, either due to fear or excitement, a monkey grimaces with clenched fists. So it is called kikhi. This habit of the monkey is prehistoric. Although the ancestors of human beings and monkeys are the same, they were separated at least one million years ago. So a human being also, when frightened or excited, clenches the fist and grimaces. A small child keeps its fist clenched most of the time, and the habit of grimacing also remains predominant in childhood. ( 2 )
Monkey leader – importance of singular leadership:

You know that some animals live in herds or groups and others live by themselves. The sheep, the lion and the elephant live collectively, but the goat, the tiger and the cat live separately, on their own. Yes, the creatures of the ape group also live collectively. All creatures with herd instinct have a leader. They do not have any form of milita netrtva [collective leadership] amongst themselves. This is because collective leadership ultimately creates fissures in the saḿgha [an association or organisation or society], and this goes against the very nature of existence. The human being is also a creature that leads a collective life. However much one might use vocal pyrotechnics or speak eloquently against hero-worship, in their heart of hearts humans have always longed for strong and firm leadership. They are collective-minded creatures; if one finds an ideal leader, one comes and offers all oneʼs love and devotion to them on the one hand, and on the other hand does not hesitate to face death willingly, at their command. This is the inner characteristic of human thinking which keeps oneʼs mind and heart always fulfilled. Even those who oppose hero-worship only do it verbally but not from the core of their heart.

In any case, these apes are a group of creatures associated with humans. Like humans, they have herd instinct and unlimited love and devotion for their leader. When the leader becomes old, he or she hands over the leadership to a younger monkey and retires. Whether they are red-faced, dark-faced or small-sized monkeys or baboons, they will have a leader. Since very ancient times, the word gabaya was used to describe a monkey leader. In spoken Bengali, we call this gabaya, viir hanumán. ( 3 )

The word kusháku, if it is used in the masculine gender, or if we spell it by using the Sanskrit spirant (visarga), then its meaning becomes “the powerful monkey” – such as viir hanumán. There are several hundred species of monkeys. They are diverse in appearance and nature. Some are calm and quiet, gentle and disciplined, and others are very brave like kushákuh. Some have a brown face and colour, others are black, and still others are red in colour. Among the red-faced monkeys, those that are smaller in appearance are called ulluk in Sanskrit. They are very intelligent. According to their degree of advancement on the evolutionary path, monkeys vary in their vocabularies. Some have only two to four hundred words in their language, and others have six to seven hundred words that they use. There is very little difference between the vocabulary size of extremely underdeveloped humans and of highly-developed monkeys. This means that if there is some addition to the vocabulary of developed monkeys, it would come close to the language of underdeveloped humans. Judging by their language, the developed monkeys with tails are more advanced than the tailless monkeys (gorillas, chimpanzees and orangutangs). Overall, of course, orangutangs have more advanced intelligence.

In physical strength none can compare with the gorillas. Among these apes, those with tails, which are more powerful – those dark-faced monkeys – are called hanumán in spoken Bengali, and in northern India languor. They have great physical strength. Male apes are called viir hanuman in colloquial language. These viir hanumáns belong to the kusháku genus. ( 4 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Leaf-hoppers (Shyámápoká): The Sanskrit word for shyamápoká is kot́ika. At the end of the rainy season, with the advent of autumn, these small insects are born in the millions and swarm across the sky and the land. Although they are very small in size, these creatures of the grasshopper suborder are very harmful for the crops. In Sanskrit they have another name, shalavá, meaning “enemy of the crops”. During early autumn they eat up the heads of the paddy crops in the fields, and in the late autumn they eat up the flowers of paddy. In ancient times, farmers found no way to save the crops from these insects. Though their onslaught continues throughout the day, they become more active when night falls, because they become irritated by sunlight.

In ancient times, farmers used to burn certain objects near the field to create fumes so as to drive them away and thereby save the crops from such an invasion. This proved barely effective. Although the fumes killed some and drove others away, they were not completely exterminated. The smoke did not harm the crops; rather it benefited them, since farmers used to fumigate the crops before flowering and not afterwards. Creating fumes amongst the barren pineapple plants causes them to bear fruit. In some countries of the world, pineapple plants are fumigated with the help of a trellis. This results very shortly in the appearance of golden pineapples.
Bon theke berola t́iye
Sońár t́opor mátháy diye.
[From the forest emerged the parrot With the golden crown on its head.]

Let us come back to the main subject. Failing to evolve any effective means to save the crops from the green leaf-hopper insects, farmers all over the world took the decision that they would arrange flames of light simultaneously during Kárttikii Amávasyá [the new moon night in the seventh month of the Bengali calendar]. The invasion of these flies would be at its worst during that time, and millions would meet their death by jumping into the flames. This configuration of lights is the prime reason behind the emergence of the festival of lights (diipávalii); other reasons for this festival came much later. The poet Candiidas has said:
Jemati diipiká ujare adhiká
Bhitare ańala shikhá,
Patauṋga ásiyá paŕaye ghuriá
Puŕiyá maraye pákhá.
[Just as the lampʼs flame burns bright, Within also burns the flame of fire, The flies circle round and then fall, With burned wings.]

In Bengali the name of this fly is shyamá or shyamápoká. The word shyamá has several meanings. Of these, the most widely accepted is “green”. You must be aware of the fact that the prince Sahasraváhu of post-Buddhist Ráŕh, conquered a large part of Southeast Asia and established a colony there. At that time, the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur (Singur – earlier in Burdawn district, now in Hoogly district). To replicate this city, he created his capital [in Southeast Asia] called Siḿhapur (or Singapur) as a city. Prince Sahasraváhu, charmed by the greenery of the entire region (Thailand), called it Shyámdesh. Even today, along with the name Thailand, its other name of Shyámdesh is also prevalent.

In any case, this insect is green in colour, due to which its name shyamá has been appropriately given. This has no connection with the goddess Shyámádevii [goddess Kali] or with Shyamápújá. Due to its green colour, these insects become lost in the greenery and create a natural camouflage of colour or natural camouflage. Although it does not have the ability of changing colour (varńa corá), it does become lost in the greenery. So it becomes very difficult to determine whether the paddy field has been invaded by these insects. In Sanskrit, of course, shyámá has other reflective connotations.
Shiit kále bhabeduśńá griiśme ca sukhashiitalá,
Atasiipuśpavarńábhá sá shyámá parikiirtiitá.
[In winter she gives warmth, in summer she gives coolness, Coloured like the atasii flower – the goddess is known as Shyámá.]

The lifespan of these insects is normally about a fortnight. Yet, after investigation it has been noted that unless there is any serious damage to their bodies or life, they can live up to two months. During the late autumn, however, due to the excessive mists, they die out. They usually lay their eggs on the upper part of grass blades. The eggs remain there for about a year. Many animals grazing in the fields eat up these eggs along with the blades of grass. Sometimes the scorching rays of the sun dry up the grass and kill the eggs. During the floods, these eggs, still attached to the blades of grass, float towards the sea. Of course, the eggs are numerous; in fact, there are millions and millions of eggs. So many of them may die [along the way], but not all. With the sprinkling of rain these eggs come to life again. At the end of the rainy season, the baby shyámápoká come out of their eggs and move about independently. They do more harm than good to humans. Yet they are food for many small-sized birds and other creatures. In that sense, they help to a great extent in maintaining the ecological balance in the world.

Nurjahan, the empress of India, was a poetess. She had a sensitive, scrutinizing mind with which she looked at all the beautiful things in life. She declared that no roses should be offered at her grave, because it would cause pain to the bulbul birds [a bird of the Pycnonotus genus] residing in the rose garden from where the roses would be plucked. She also said that no lamps should be lit there because in the flames, countless green flies would be burnt to death. She would not be able to endure it.
Gariib gore keu dviip jveloná
Sájáiyo ná keu gule,
Shyámápokár ná poŕe pákhá
Dágá ná páya bulbule.
[Do not light any lamp on this poor oneʼs grave, Do not arrange any bouquets here; Let not any green insect burn its wings here, Nor any bulbul feel pained on my account.] ( 1 )]
Locust (pauṋgapál): The meaning of the word kot́ika is shalabhá (locust), in Bengali pauṋgapál, in northern India t́id́d́i, and in Bhojpuri t́iiṋŕii.

Pauṋgapál (locust) is a peculiar kind of insect. Generally it appears only in desert areas on occasion, when sultry weather abounds. You know, the heat of the desert is usually dry. Surely you must be aware of the fact that the heat of Jodhpur is much more intense than that of Kolkata. Yet the Kolkata climate, because of greater humidity, causes people to sweat profusely. Due to this perspiration, excessive salt exudes from the body and this weakens the power of activity. More than Kolkata, in East and North Bengal this sultriness is even more intense. So according to the theory of East and Wet ( 2 ) [humidity factor], the people of East and North Bengal are less industrious than those of Ráŕh. Again, the people of Assam suffer more from humid climate than those of East and North Bengal. That is why the people of Assam are far less industrious. Although the heat of Jodhpur is more intense than that of Kolkata, there is hardly any humidity. That is why there is less sweating and therefore less fatigue. While staying in Rajasthan, I personally experienced this. In any case, even in this desert region, if there is one percent increase in humidity, the locusts increase by the millions. In fact, locust eggs lie in a dormant state for several years in the desert, and once it becomes humid they bloom into life. This happens not only in Rajasthan, in Thar (Sindh), in the northern desert regions of Gujarat, but also in Persia (Iran), Baluchistan, Sahara and Gobi. Even in the deserts of South America such phenomena occur to some extent.

Though locusts are very close to grasshoppers as a suborder of insects, there is hardly any similarity in their nature or habits. The habitat of grasshoppers, especially their birthplace, is the extensive sandy beds of large rivers. They cannot, however, live far from a humid environment. They live in verdant fields and eat green leaves. Thus as a natural camouflage, their colour is deep green. Similarly, locusts are insects that feed on leaves of grass. However, because they are born in deserts, their colour is different. Bengal is far away from deserts, and so there are scarcely any locust attacks in Bengal. In assessing their nature and habits, the primary difference between grasshoppers and locusts is that grasshoppers do not live in groups, while locusts always do so. When they fly together in the millions, their dark shadow overcasts the sky. Whatever region they fly over finds its vegetation destroyed. These shalabhá or locusts are food for human beings in certain regions of the earth.

Yogiráj [king of yogis] Matsyendranath was a prince of the erstwhile East Bengal. Moynamati was the capital of Shriibhúmi (British Tripura – now Coomilla district of present Bangladesh). Since the pre-Buddhist era, this Moynamati was famous for handwoven yarns, especially for colourful shirts. This prince was the inventor of the yogic postures Matsyendrásan [twist posture], and Shalabhásan [locust posture]. In Shalabhásana, people look like locusts, and hence the name.

Moynamati was the mother of Yogiráj Matsyendranath. She not only raised her son, but also ruled this kingdom in Bengal as regent until her son came of age. She is still remembered with deep love and respect. ( 3 )

Grasshopper (gauṋgáphaŕiḿ): Grasshoppers are quite large in size. There are certain similarities in the appearance of these creatures and of locusts; of course, there are more dissimilarities between them. The Sanskrit word for locust is shalabhá, which can be spelt with s or sh or śa.

As told earlier the birthplace of locusts is the desert. There are some wet and humid places in the desert. It must be understood that the water table in those areas is comparatively high. Sometimes an oasis is close by (even if an oasis is not near, it can be created by the artesian effect). Locusts lay their legs under the leaves of thorny plants or under a layer of sand. The eggs do not hatch regularly. In certain years, due to severe dust storms or from enhanced humidity in the atmosphere, the eggs burst forth in millions and give birth to young ones, which grow very rapidly. They then move out in search of green corn fields. Locusts born in the desert of Rajasthan usually fly away towards the fields of Eastern India, and to the north in Punjab and Haryana. Only a few fly southwards. Some people eat these locusts.

The case of grasshoppers is somewhat different. Large plants grow on the sandy beds of the Ganges or large rivers. Grasshoppers lay their eggs under the leaves of these plants. If excessively humid air blows there, the eggs thrive and give birth to nymphs. Usually they move within a five mile radius of the banks of large rivers (the Ganges and other rivers). In other words, they love to move in those places near the humid atmosphere of the river. Sometimes they can even be found close to small rivers. They do not move to the hills or far away from the riverbeds. Almost every year their eggs hatch and give birth to babies.

The number of grasshoppers increases during any year in which there is greater rainfall or more humidity. They are fond of eating green leaves. As a natural camouflage, their body is green like the leaves. Thus when they are sitting on greenery or on leaves, it is difficult to discover these grasshoppers. The opportunity exists for all grasshoppers in natural surroundings to become lost in the midst of the green leaves. Locusts are creatures of the desert, and hence their colour matches that of the desert. Once in our childhood, millions of locusts flew over Bihar and northern Bengal towards China. I remember that for a few minutes darkness descended everywhere. The blue sky was overcast with locusts.

Locusts live in groups, but grasshoppers normally live singly. Sometimes it is found that grasshoppers are longer in appearance than locusts. Physically however, locusts are sturdier than grasshoppers. They can eat more than grasshoppers. God gives with one hand and takes with another. In the ancient science of agriculture, some of the enemies of crop cultivation mentioned are excessive rainfall, drought, political revolution, crop diseases and locusts; but the droppings of locusts are very good fertilizers.

The postures of grasshoppers sitting and flying are somewhat like that of horses that stop suddenly while running or when they begin to run. That is why in Bihar, especially in Magadha, the grasshopper is called Rámjiike ghoŕá [Lord Ramʼs horse]. ( 4 )

Cricket (ucciḿŕe): The meaning of kośaja is “any creature born of eggs” – specifically lizards, and more specifically, ucciḿŕe or ghurńiipoká or crickets. Ucciḿŕe is an insect of the locust or shalabhá family. Of course, for shalabhá, the right environment is the desert. Their eggs give rise to nymphs in the desert after just a few days of wet or cloudy weather. It is not the same with grasshoppers (pauṋgapál). They grow in each and every country. Of course, wet and soft soil is the proper breeding ground for grasshoppers. The rainy season is their favourite season. Another point of difference between shalabhá and grasshoppers is that the former are fond of green leaves and trees. Hence although born in the desert, they then migrate to green fields and vegetation. Grasshoppers normally do not do so. They remain in whichever country they are born. They are also very fond of the green leaves of trees, but are not averse to other kinds of food.

Grasshoppers do not try to bite humans; in contrast, people in certain countries catch them in countless swarms by throwing nets, store them in baskets and then eat them. Crickets also do not normally bite people, and they are not eaten by people in any country. However, people in certain countries do eat locusts and other insects of the grasshopper suborder. According to some people, St. John [the Baptist] lived on grasshoppers dipped in honey during his simple, unassuming life. I do not know how far this is true, but one should not be surprised, since in ancient times humans did eat insects, particularly when they did not yet know the art of cultivation or did not know how to use fire. In the Vedas it is mentioned:
Niilah patauṋgo harito lohitákśa
stad́idgarbha rtavah samudráh,
Anádimattvaḿ vibhutvena vartase yato játáni
bhutáni vishvá.

[Little blue insects, little green insects, and red-eyed birds; clouds full of thunder and lightning; the seasons, the ocean – all these manifestations of Yours – proclaim Your power from beginningless time.] ( 5 )]
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Bee: The word náyaka means “one who leads”. Kośanáyaka means “one who carries weapons” or “the carrier of weapons or treasures who does it for the sake of preservation”. So, one of the literal meanings of kośanáyaka is the Apis indica type of bee. In India there are three types of bees (maomáchi): rock bee, bush bee and Apis indica. Rock bee is a large bee species that produces honey in large quantities. They have large honeycombs, normally on banyan trees or other large trees. Sometimes the honeycombs are so large that they break apart, and the honey oozes out and drips onto the ground. The honey produced by the rock bees is somewhat pungent. It is known as ugraviirja [inducing vitality]. When human vitality is reduced, when the coldness of death descends upon oneʼs exhausted body, many a time this type of honey called ugraviirja comes to instil new life and energy.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: In a human body that has reduced vitality, so long as there is no blood-consuming disease, ten drops of this particular honey, if consumed in the morning along with the leaves of krśńa-tulasii [black basil] on an empty stomach, will yield excellent results. However if a person has blood dysentery or any ulcer in the body, then one must not take it. The honey must be sucked [or licked], not swallowed. That is why in Indian ayurvedic science it is called avaleha.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: Bush bees are small-sized bees. They are ancient inhabitants of India. Instead of building honeycombs on trees, they prefer to build them on the walls of mud houses. In the villages of Ráŕh Bengal, when ants make their home in mud houses built with clayish soil, if the bush bees find an opportunity to occupy them, they build their choicest and most beautiful honeycombs there. We obtain minimum honey from such individual honeycombs; but the honey is well-refined and pleasant in taste and scent. On the other hand, it is lower in vitality than any other honey. Good quality neem honey (obtained from the neem flower) is produced by these bees. It is surmised that they are the original bees of Ráŕh Bengal. They do not sting readily. Even when they sting, there is hardly that unbearable pain which is caused by the sting of rock bees.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: Apis indica are the original bees of India. They are medium in size and live in medium-sized trees. Some trees produce floral nectar in plenty, and these bees build their honeycombs there or in neighbouring areas. If there is no fear of enemies, they build their honeycombs on the lower branches of trees. They are found all over Bengal; but they are mostly seen in large numbers in southern Bengal; especially in southern Ráŕh. They can fly for a long distance. Their stings cause severe pain. They prepare good honey from mustard flowers. At one time physicians preferred honey produced by these bees in the preparation of ayurvedic medicines. The very name Apis indica denotes their identity as the original bees of India. In Ráŕh they normally build their honeycombs in areas adjacent to rivers or at the confluence of rivers, mostly on trees of medium height. In the Sundarbans at the end of winter, they are the first to come forward to begin building their honeycombs. The wax of these honeycombs is quite pliable and soft. There was a time when it was sold at a very high price. Another good name of these Apis indica bees is kośanáyaka. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: Wasp and hornet (boltá and bhiimrul): The hornet is such a creature that wherever it goes it builds a honeycomb nearby, so it is very much prone to building shelters. That is why one meaning of the word grhakárii is “hornet”. The difference between the wasp and the hornet is that the former is lean, thin and yellowish in colour, while the latter is stout and sturdy and has a reddish band near the waist. The sting of the hornet is more painful than that of the wasp. As far as I understand, the word bhiimrul has come from bhiim (severe) and hul (sting). Instead of hul, the villagers of Ráŕh pronounce it as rul. In Sanskrit, boltá is called baŕat́á, in Hindi baŕre; the Sanskrit word for bhiimrul is grhakárii, in Hindi, birńii. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: White ant: Ui [white ant] is a native Bengali word. In North India, diimak is used; on the Bengal and North India border, diiyaṋk or diiyáṋ is used; in English ui means “white-ant”, and in Sanskrit valmiikakiit́a or pluśińa is used. In many parts of Bengal, a is used in place of ra, and ra is used in place of a. For this reason ui are called rui nearly everywhere in southern Bengal. The mushroom that grows on anthills is called rui-chátu [ant-mushroom]. This tiny creature belonging to the ant group increases its numbers at an extremely fast rate. They cannot see anything in the sunlight. Their sense of touch also diminishes when exposed to sunlight. Thus they build little tunnels out of the earth to protect themselves from sunlight and use them to move around in because their sense of touch and other senses come to life in the darkness of these tunnels. Under certain conditions, the different branches and sub-branches of these tunnels that they construct right and left become visible as a mound or hillock. In spoken Bengali we call this ui-dhibi, in English “anthill”, in Sanskrit valmiika. An anthill was built around the entire body of a sage who remained motionless for many days during the practice of his austerities. At the time that he sat for meditation, he was known by the name of Ratnákara. The people gave him the name Válmiiki because at the time that he finished his penance and rose from his seat, his body was encased in an anthill.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: People in many countries of the world eat ants – even civilized people in some places. They say that ants are tasty and have a sweet and sour flavour.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: In Sanskrit the word pluśińa was more widely used than the word valmiikakiit́a. Sama pluśińa sama mashakena sama nágena sama ebhistribhirlokaeh, that is, Parama Puruśa is unbiased. He is equal to everyone because He sees everyone in the same way. He sees an ant in the same way He sees a small mosquito. He understands an ant in the same way that He understands a mosquito. He does not make any undue fuss over a giant serpent (python or “elephant of the jungle”) because of its great size. He sees a python or “elephant of the jungle” in the same way that He sees an ant or a mosquito, and they also see Him in that same way. Nor does He make any special fuss over this universe, the three worlds of heaven, earth and hell, because of their vastness, and they also look at Him in the same way. In other words, everyone is equal to Parama Puruśa – a mosquito, ant, python, mammoth and even the three worlds. He remains with everyone equally through His ota yoga and prota yoga [individual and collective association of Parama Purnśa with jiiva]. He is impartial under all conditions.
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: In the opinion of biologists, ants first appeared on the earth approximately six million years ago. It is possible that they appeared somewhat earlier than this, but not later. In other words, after ants arrived on the earth, they passed through at least one, if not more than one, ice age, and have arrived in their present form having undergone one or more long hibernations. ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
chapterTitle: Bees, Wasps and Hornets, and White Ants

t: Bugs (kit́ibha): Kit́ibha: kit́i+bha+d́a = kit́ibha. The etymological meaning of the word kit́ibha is “that which looks like a kit́i”. In common usage, kit́ibha means “bug”. There are two reasons why a bug is called kit́ibha. Suppose you have returned very tired… It is already night … you are about to sleep. Then suddenly you notice a bug on your bed. Well, you might have immediately killed the bug. But you are left with the apprehension that since you have spotted one bug, there must be more bugs in the bed. You say to yourself, “I will lose my sleep for nothing tonight.” You are frightened by the bleak prospect of spending an agonizing night. The kind of fear that you experience on seeing the bug is similar to the kind of fear you have on seeing a rhino or a boar. So a bug is called kit́ibha, that is, like a kit́i [rhino].

In ancient times people used to say that there is another reason for calling a bug kit́ibha. That is, if you look at a bug through a magnifying glass, making it fifty or hundred times larger than its actual size, you will see that it is a creature of horrifying appearance. Howsoever brave and valorous you may be, you are sure to be frightened by the terrible sight of the hugely magnified bug. That is why another name for bug is kit́ibha. ( 1 )

Large-sized scorpion: Khararomańa means “large-sized, dark and hairy scorpion” (in English scorpion, in Latin scorpio). Usually these scorpions live in the hills. They live in the openings between rocks or in large crevices in the hills. These dark-coloured scorpions are known as khararomańa. They are very venomous. In 1963 the present writer was once bitten by such a scorpion. Its sting is unbearably painful. Small babies might succumb to their sting. Once in the khirkhiriá section of the Rajmahal branch of Ramgarh hills [Jamalpur hills fall in the same hill range] there were plenty of these scorpions. In my boyhood days I used to watch these scorpions bristling together, removing slabs of stone. At that time, that particular hill was covered with forests. Later the hill and the forest came under control of the provincial government (state government). During the British rule, the forests were ruined. As a result such scorpions also quickly became extinct. In 1964 when I went there, I saw that the number of these scorpions was greatly reduced in the forests, and even removing the stone slabs I could hardly come across one or two such creatures. Their number must have been even further reduced, since there is no forest in that area now. In the plains adjacent to the hills, due to abolition of the zamindary system, the forests have been obliterated. Arrangements have been made for sanctuaries, only for the sake of preserving certain wild animals. However, since no preservation of these scorpions is possible, they will soon become extinct.

In this context, let me point out that these scorpions are the favourite food of long-beaked birds, such as cranes, adjutant storks and parrots (especially wild parrots or bon-tiyá), which attack them en masse and eat them up. ( 2 )

The word kurpii means káṋkŕá biche [crab scorpion; it derives its name from the Bengali word káṋkŕá which means crab]. Its alternative Sanskrit name is briscika. The etymological meaning of the word brishcika is something of a crooked nature. Another meaning of the word is “something which is unbearable”. The Bengali word bichá or biche is derived from the word brishcika. There are several different species of scorpions in the world. The chief among them are teṋtule biche [a variety of scorpions as dark-coloured as a ripe tamarind seed] and káṋkŕá biche. Although teṋtule biche can be of different colours, it is mainly reddish in appearance. And when it lies quietly on the road, from a distance it looks like a ripe tamarind seed. Hence its name is teṋtule biche. In India, apart from a good number of white and yellow varieties of teṋtule biche, a genus of ink-black colour is also found. Many people call a white scorpion sarasvatii biche [Saraswati is a mythological Hindu deity, whose colour is supposed to be pure white], a yellow scorpion or sońá biche [golden-coloured scorpion], and the black scorpion or káli biche [dark-coloured scorpion like the dark-complexioned mythological Hindu goddess Káli].

The biting power of all scorpions is not the same. The sting of some results in a heavy loss of blood, whereas in the case of others the loss is minimal. These scorpions are venomous no doubt, but the burning sensation that their bite causes is not entirely due to the venom; it is mainly due to loss of blood. A scorpion is far more venomous than a teṋtule biche. The way in which a scorpion moves resembles somewhat that of a crab. Hence it is called káṋkŕá biche. When a crab moves, it keeps its claws raised all along. This is because it moves with the thought that if it is attacked by an approaching enemy, it will launch a counter attack immediately. The same is the case with a scorpion. It also moves with its claws elevated, so that it can collide with an advancing enemy and pierce its sting into its body. In India, generally three types of scorpions are found: 1) pale-dark, 2) deep-dark, and 3) those dwelling on hills and mountains. The pale-dark variety is somewhat smaller in size, and its bite is less painful. In Bengal, this type of scorpion found in greater number. The deep-dark variety is larger in size, and its bite is extremely painful. If it bites a child, it can even cause the childʼs death. They are sometimes found to live in the holes between the leaves of banana trees. Those who incise date-palm trees are often attacked by this type of scorpion.

The hill scorpions normally dwell in hills in narrow openings between large-sized pieces of rock. Some of these scorpions have hair on their body. Their bite is very painful. The venom of scorpions is used in poison therapy. Its venom is also used in the preparation of homeopathic medicines. The old Sanskrit and Vedic name of scorpions is kurpii. The name brishcika is also quite old. Their Latin equivalent is ‘scorpio’. From ‘scorpio’ has come the English word ‘scorpion’. The word kaorpya means anything related to scorpions.
