You can call the venom of scorpions kaorpya viśa, and the medicine prepared from its venom kaorpya aosadha. You can also call a man of extremely crooked nature kaorpya kut́ila.
Among the zodiac signs, next to Libra is Scorpio. It looks almost like a scorpion with its claws raised. ( 3 )

Louse (ukun): Keshakiit́a (louse) is a type of insect which resides in hair and eats the fat at the root of the hair and the skin of the head. Literally, it means “louse”. The eggs of the louse are called niki and the adult lice are called dyáuṋgar. So you understand the meaning of the word “louse,” and you must be alert regarding these insects. In earlier times, to protect themselves from lice attack, people used to blend kerosene oil with coconut oil in equal proportions and apply it on the head. It was necessary to sit with oneʼs back to the sun for one hour in this condition before taking bath. That resulted in the disappearance of the lice in two or three days. Nowadays one can do the same or use [lice] shampoo once a month to protect oneself from the onslaught of lice. ( 4 )

Gandhi bug: In the equatorial region there resides a particular type of insect which is known as gándhipoká, from whose body emanates a pungent smell. It tends to fill the adjoining areas with a foul smell, for which reason house lizards do not come near them – nor do other creatures that normally prey upon insects. In certain situations, these insects cause tremendous harm to contain crops. Of course, they are also beneficial to other crops.

Mosquito: The d́áṋsh [gnat] variety of mosquito (mashá) can drink excessive quantities of blood. After they drink an excessive quantity of blood they remain torpid for quite some time. Some are of the opinion that their stomach often bursts and they die as a result of drinking too much blood.
The d́áṋsh variety of mosquito is called “gnat” in English. Karvva also means “gnat.” [One should] use the word karvá for “female gnat”, rather than the word karvii. ( 5 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Rat: Kund + uń = kundu. The etymological meaning is “one whose nature is to lurk”. Suppose there are seven hundred rats in a room. A cat enters the room. The rats immediately know it; they understand the situation. Suddenly, from that very moment, they stop all movement, stop making any noise. Silence reigns in the room. It would be hard for anyone to know that seven hundred rats were lurking. So one colloquial meaning of the word kundu is a rat of any kind, whether a rat or a mouse. In Hindi a rat is called cuhá and a mouse is called cuhiyá. In Bihar the big ones are called muś, the small ones cut́ri. For a woodland rat or field mouse the word ákhu was common in old Sanskrit. In later times the word went almost completely out of use. Múśika or iṋdura refers to all kinds of rodents. Muśá was common in old Bengali. Now it has gone out of use.
Bháńd́árete rákhá chilo páli chaya dhán,
Ganesher muśáte karila jalapán.
[There were six pots of rice in the storehouse, The mouse of Ganesha made a good meal out of them.]

There is a particular community that is known as “Muśáhara” because they eat rats. Generally in Bihar large rats are called muśá and medium-sized rats are called muśa. These words are not used in standard Hindi and Urdu, however. ( 1 )

As you well know, there are many species of iṋdur such as the mouse, the rat, the field mouse [marmot group], tree rat, etc. Some of them live in kitchens, some in storerooms, some in holes in the wall and some in tree hollows. They have many names according to their species and dwelling place: iṋdur, muśika, ákhu, kundu, and so on. The mole also has three main species in India. But they are all field moles; they live in burrows in the fields. The entrance to the burrow is towards the bottom and the burrow itself moves upward. So what happens is that during heavy rains when the field is on the point of being submerged, it is difficult for water to seep into the dwelling. If there is water at the mouth of the hole, they can easily come out and escape. Since it lives in a field, the moleʼs proper name is vasumitra. During the day the mole cannot see properly, so they mostly come out at night. Certainly you will hardly ever see a mole entering your house during the day. You see it at night.

The moleʼs burrow is also called kulaka. One proper name for the mole is kulakeya, in the sense of “kulaka-dweller”, kulakeyii in feminine gender. Do you not call “the mole” that type of firework which runs about hither and thither during Diipavali [light festival] just like a mole does, making a sharp hissing sound? This mole firework does not stay in a kulaka; it is kept in a box or in oneʼs pocket. The moleʼs hole is called kulaka, but do you know the name of the ratʼs hole? It is good that you do. If you do not know, then listen well. The word is kundubil. Kundu means “rat;” bil means “hole” or “opening”. The word bil is used in Hindi and in a few North Indian languages to mean “hole”. ( 2 )

One who goes around all the time looking for or eating something or the other is karvva. Rats are always going around looking for food. If they do not find anything edible they will cut things with their teeth, thinking that after it is cut up it might turn into food. In this sense, the word karvva also means “rat.” Of course, karvva does not mean “mouse” (plural, “mice”). ( 3 )

Aromatic rat (gandhamuśika): You are already familiar with the word “hibernation”. You all know that there are cold-blooded creatures on this earth. They cannot move or function in cold weather. That is why they fall asleep for a long spell with the advent of winter. They feel drowsy two or three days before their hibernation starts. At that time, struggling against drowsiness, they move towards a safe shelter and lie down. Generally that shelter is under the ground, because they feel warm there. That warmth of the ground does not allow them to die. During this long spell of sleep, they consume the fat (in Bengali basá, carbi in Hindustani) accumulated in their body. At the end of winter, the lukewarm weather of spring creates a stir in their nerves and blood, and they awake. If someone kills them while they are in hibernation, they die, but their sleep does not break. That is why this hibernation is described in Sanskrit as himanidrá. After this long spell of sleep they emerge from their hole in the ground. Due to the reduced fat in the body, the upper layer of their skin slackens, just as happens with a fat person after a spell of sickness, or with a person who has crossed over from middle age into old age.

So, on waking from hibernation, these creatures shed the loose skin from their body. The skin they shed is called khosá, or outer skin, just like the outer skin of the coconut or the banana skin. In the language of Kolkata Bengali it is called kholá – that which can be removed. In Bengal both the words kholá and khosá are widely used. That which has to be removed, which cannot be kept on the body even though one might like to keep it, and the removal of which is indispensable, is called kholas in Bengali. So after getting up from hibernation these creatures shed their skin (kholash). The chaste Bengali or Sanskrit word for this kholash is nirmok. So it is said, “Snakes shed their skin in the spring.” When the old skin is shed, the inner skin that emerges is very thin and sensitive. At this time, the creatures cannot bear the scorching rays of the sun. So they come out of their hole only in the early hours of the night. Now, during the spring and summer seasons, there is a greater intrusion of snakes onto village roads. Since their skin has become sensitive, if anyone tramples upon them, they strike. So when moving about at night on the road during this period, one must carry some kind of light.

Be that as it may, these cold-blooded creatures in India are appreciable in number. At the end of Ashvin or Kárttik [end of autumn] they lie down to hibernate. Chief amongst those who indulge in this form of hibernation is a small creature of the rodent order that lives in the holes of the lower Himalayan mountain ranges. They are generally known as marmots. A strange odour emanates from their body. The chaste Bengali name for such aromatic rats is gandhamuśika. ( 4 )

Otter (udbiŕála): Uda or udaka means “water”. The etymological meaning of udbiŕála is “that cat-like creature that lives in the water”. Its colloquial meaning is bhodaŕ [otter]. Some people have the notion that this otter [Mustelid family] is perhaps an aquatic creature, but it is not. It is a land creature like the crocodile and the fish-eating crocodile. It goes into the water to catch prey. It is a land-dwelling creature that breastfeeds its young. It sleeps and gives birth on land, and it normally lives in large holes near ponds and reservoirs. ( 5 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

When the large animals of ancient times became physically incapacitated, they took refuge in a secluded place and died there in the normal course of events. According to some scholars, the bones and fat of these animals accumulated in those places. Some form of terrible whirlpools were created in the sea, in watersheds or large lakes, and due to that, the remains of the dead animals inside those whirlpools would drift out to sea and become the Sargasso Sea (Saraságar or floating islands of earth). They even floated into the ocean depths. Some scholars believe that those places where earlier saraságars were created from the remains of animal bodies now yield us oil [petrol] from under the earth. If such places, instead of being close to the sea, happened to be inside any land region, then the fat and other remains of these large animals would float out to the sea, whereas the bones would pile up in the form of hills. In the course of time, these hills of bones turned into limestone or dolomite.

When this calcium-enriched substance was burned, it turned into a type of lime, which we call in spoken language páthure cuń [lime obtained by calcination]. When the shells of water-grown animals with hard skin (snails, oysters, conch shells, etc) are turned into a type of lime through calcination, we describe it in spoken language as kalicuń. In southern Bengal the whitewashing of houses is called kali pheráno [bringing new lime]. A commercial centre developed for this kind of lime along with matted coir ( 1 ) has come to be known today as Kalikátá [Kolkata] – in Oriya language Kalikatá. Another village near this place is also called Kalikátá. Whether it is lime produced by calcination or kalicuń, both are produced from the bones of animal bodies. Those who are averse to taking kalicuń in betel leaf [for chewing after a meal], thinking that it is produced from an animal body, should remember that the calcinated lime (páthure cuń) is also derived from animal bodies. Not only the leader of the elephant herd but all elephants belonging to herds in the forest used to go into such seclusion as death neared. Today elephants do not have permanent habitats. Fearing human beings, they move from one forest to another, hence they also have no fixed place to breathe their last breath. ( 2 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Animals in the world have their different styles of movement. The ant moves quickly but keeps it eyes open for any sweets, sugar or other food morsels along the way. Usually nothing lying on its path escapes attention. Since it has a limited number of senses, it must perform the function of several senses using a sensitive nose.

The tiger moves very cautiously, keeping its eyes on both sides of the path so as to take note of anything unusual happening. If it notices that certain objects are lying on its path which it did not see earlier, it will keep its eyes alert while moving towards it, and if it senses that things are unfamiliar and unsafe, it will shun that path. The tiger is a very clever animal. As it falls upon its prey and moves away with it, it runs very swiftly and leaps also. The movement of the cat may not be exactly like that of the tiger, but there are great similarities between them.

The horse usually runs continuously. When taking a turn to the left or the right, it is hardly aware of propriety. The pig never moves in a disciplined manner; whatever food it comes across, it turns in that direction. The dog usually moves quickly. Although it runs in the direction of food, it does not at all lack alertness. The buffalo moves more slowly than the cow, while always fixing its eyes on the watershed. When it comes across any watershed, it does not care for any right or wrong and simply plunges into the water. The cow normally moves at a medium pace and habitually avoids mud, slime, water and sand very carefully. It does not like to come in contact with water, and does not like to bathe in water at all. The lion is fond of moving in leaps and bounds. It also loves to run. However, it has less intelligence. So for no real reason it runs and leaps and thereby endangers itself.

Sheep move at a medium pace and prefer to move in a row. The first sheep in the row may keep its eyes on food but others in the row follow the beaten track blindly. This movement of sheep is called gad́d́áliká praváha [following the beaten track] or gad́d́ál > gad́hál > gáŕhol >gáŕol. The foolish person is sarcastically called gáŕol. Actually gáŕol means “sheep”. In northern India, those who tend the sheep are known as gad́heri.
Aesii gatii saḿsár kii sab gaŕhar kii t́hát́
Ek jab gáŕh me giire sab játa tehi bát́.
[The nature of people is somewhat like that of a flock of sheep. When one sheep falls into a ditch, the others will follow.]

In this world, there is a common trend. Just as one sheep runs ahead, the other sheep behind it follow suit. If the sheep ahead falls into a pit, the sheep behind it also fall into the pit. The ox loves to move haltingly. After moving forward a few steps, it stands still like a sculpted statue. If it happens to notice any food nearby, it will slowly move in that direction without caring what others might think. It does not even care to check whether someone may come chasing it. Its temperament is such that it appears not to care for anyone on this earth. Suppose you see an ox standing on the road. For your own safety, you are walking at a distance by the side of a drain on the other side of the road. The ox would not even bother to look at you; it simply would have no interest. However, if you are wearing a garland of marigolds around your neck, it will advance towards you. You might think it is coming to knock you down, and so you may run away. However, the ox is not coming to attack you. It is coming in your direction to snatch away the marigolds and gobble them up. The habit of the ox is to move step by step and then halt, rest a while, and then again move. Due to this strange habit it is called kramodbeg [graded tension]. This word is specifically used to describe an ox of bulky appearance. ( 1 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

Crocodiles develop friendships with sparrows and other tiny birds, while donkeys are friends with pigeons. On the sandy beds of rivers the crocodile rests and warms itself in the sun, keeping its mouth open while tiny birds enter its mouth and pick up bits of meat from in between its teeth, thus cleansing them. It is to be remembered that the crocodile does not use any kind of toothbrush or other instrument to clean its teeth. Likewise, pigeons sitting on the backs of donkeys pick lice and other insects and eat them. The donkeys feel comfortable with this and the pigeons also obtain their supply of food. Donkeys feel much better when the pigeons have picked the insects off their backs. That is why pigeons are the favorite birds of donkeys. For this reason, pigeons are also known as kharapriya. ( 1 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

I mentioned to you in connection with musk that the hormone secreted by the musk deer accumulates in its navel, and as it becomes stiffer, the intensity of its fragrance also increases. Ultimately when it becomes too stiff, the fragrance also becomes too intense. At this stage, overwhelmed and excited by the fragrance, the deer runs madly in search of the fragrance until finally, exhausted and worn out, it meets its death. Similarly the elephant, in a state of frenzy in certain situations, turns mad and after some time it dies. Of course, not all elephants turn mad, and those which do become mad do not live long in this condition. Among elephants, such deaths are not frequent, yet they do occur. Elephants that go berserk are not only dangerous for human beings; they are also dangerous for other elephants. Other elephants become frightened of them and stay far away. In normal conditions, elephants enter human localities in search of food. Their favorite food is green leaves and twigs, ripe maize, paddy and wheat. If they can procure food without any disturbance, they do not attack anyone. The villagers light fires and beat drums and tin pots; they do all these things not in fear but to avoid any kind of disturbance.

When an elephant goes berserk, it does not even think of food; it goes without food for several days and even goes without water. Its overheated brain urges it to break laws... to challenge restrictions. You all know that there are those who encourage people to break laws, and in fact incite them to do so. The consequences are never good. To quickly achieve independence during British rule, a class of political leaders started a civil disobedience movement (in Hindi, kánun toŕńá). Some of them used to say, “Our objective is not to break the law … our aim is to tear through the mist of darkness to reveal the truth … to snatch our freedom away from the clutches of evil; this is not a movement to break laws.” This is our urge, our search for truth… this is satyágraha [the movement for truth].

However, whatever name you may give to the rose, the rose is still a rose… The thresher still threshes paddy even while in heaven… this path of disobeying the law is the way to break the law… to challenge any regulation. Its results are never good. Today, following in this tradition, without any forethought, for the slightest agitation, for any dissatisfaction, people burn trams and buses which were purchased with the tax-payerʼs money… they burn down private and state buildings, destroying their own hard-earned wealth, and reduce them to ashes. Behind all these acts lies that old civil disobedience movement of those unruly people during the British rule – or what can be called in chaste language “satyágraha.” After careful analysis and discrimination, we should call it “durágraha” [movement for evil] and not a movement for truth. Rather it is a tool to destroy the present society.

Those who, in the name of revolution or “leftism” kill innocent people, who are devoid of reason, and who, under the impetus of their confused, irrational philosophy lose their humanity, are also goaded and misguided by a similar type of psychology.

Be that as it may, I have already said too much in the context of the elephant gone berserk. Nature does not approve of breaking laws. So long as there are rules and regulations, they must be observed. If they are found to be harmful, if they impede the progress of society, if they try to encircle, entangle and shackle the path of human progress at every step like a snake entwined about oneʼs legs, in that case, they must be smashed and razed to dust. New laws must be enacted and obeyed. Otherwise there will be anarchy; the law of big fish eating little fish will dominate society. The civil disobedience movement in India has left that kind of harmful impact on the Indian society.

However, in the case of the musk deer, when it dies in this state of frenzy, usually, the navel of the deer is extracted from its body and used for therapeutic purposes. In ancient times, people believed that when a person developed breathing difficulties in the final critical stage [of life], the use of the navel hormone of the musk deer increases the body temperature and sometimes the person even survives. Whether the person survives or not, their life is prolonged, although only for a brief period; there is no doubt about it. The medicinal power and quality that makaradhvaja [aquaregia] has are also present to a somewhat greater extent in musk. It is very potent indeed.

From this musk, several products are manufactured. However, before production the navel of the musk deer must be reduced to a powder. This powdered navel is called gand́hadhuli [the powder of fragrant musk]. ( 1 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

The elephant is very capricious. Many years ago I once fell victim to the whims of an elephant and was in deep trouble (nestnábud: nástánábud used in Bengali is incorrect; either nistnábud or nestnábud can be used). It was towards the end of the month of Áshvin or the beginning of Kárttik [mid-October]. I ( 1 ) had gone to Arrah to take part in a conference. At that time Arrah was the headquarters of Sahabad District. In ancient times, the northern part of Sahabad District was known as Árańyadesh (the name Arrah originated from that], and the southern part was known as Rohitarájya (named after King Harishchandraʼs son, Rohitáshva). To the north of Sahabad lay the Gauṋgá, on its eastern border was the Sone River, on its western border the Karmanáshá River and to the south the Vindhya Mountains. When emperor Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subáh [provinces], he cut a portion from the province of Bengal and created a new province which he named Bihar. Sahabad was a district in that province; Arrah was its headquarters. Shershah Surii was an illustrious son of Sahabad; his tomb is in Sasaram. (Actually Sahasrarám or Sahasrám or Sasaram comes from the name Sahasraram Singh.)

The name Sahabad comes from Shershah; the Paraganá [former administrative division in India] within Malda District, which contained Gaoŕa, the capital of Bengal, was named Shershahabad Paragana after Shershah. Although it is the headquarters of a very large district, Arrah is a mid-sized rather than a very large city. However, it has a flourishing market.

When I got down at Arrah station, I saw that a large procession was there to take me from the station. It had elephants at the front and behind them horses, behind the horses motorcycles and behind the motorcycles rows of bicycles. The elephant that had been chosen for me was an aerávat [a very big elephant like the renowned mammoth] of a local mahárájá [king]. It was tall and imposing with a litter on its back. On the litter was the mahárájáʼs throne, fashioned of silver and studded with jewels.

The elephant was sitting to the north of the station. Even though he was sitting, I needed a ladder to be able to climb up. On the litter, a silver wall encircled the throne. On the wall there were small, coloured bulbs to magnify the resplendence of the procession.

The procession started off in a timely fashion. We were going down Arrahʼs main market road with the band out in front. The grandeur of the procession was especially worth seeing. When the elderly people saw it, they said that the city of Arrah had never before seen such a colourful procession. And such a magnificently decorated elephant had never passed through there before. Several motorcycles were travelling beside me. In front was the car that had been arranged for me. At the right moment the bulbs around me lit up. It increased the radiance indeed, but the heat of the bulbs in that month of October made me damp with sweat. It was my first experience of such a fierce radiance.

The procession continued on and on. Travelling along the public thoroughfare to the beat of the band, the elephantʼs bulky feet began to dance. Its speed slackened. With its dancing beat, the mahout at the front and myself behind were bouncing up and down incessantly.
We were going along well. There were a great number of people taking part in the procession. Their loud noise rent the skies.
But providence is unfavourable!

Suddenly I saw an electric wire running from one side [of the road] to the other. Its height was a little lower than that of the elephant. The litter was even higher, and still higher was the throne. And on top of that, there I was, even higher still!

The danger was right in front of us. If four feet or so could have been cut off from the legs of the elephant from the ground upwards, then perhaps it might have been possible to avoid the danger of the wire, but that would also create a problem. If its legs were cut, then the elephant would no longer be able to move, let alone dance. The mahout was beating the elephant on its head with the goad, saying, “Sit Sam, sit Sam, sit Sam.” Who was listening to whom? The elephant was at that moment in another world. He was busy dancing to the beat of the band. The command of the mahout did not even reach his ears.

The participants in the procession sensed the impending danger. One of them quickly took off his dhoti and folded it. Four strong men caught each of the four corners of the folded dhoti with their two hands holding on tightly. Incidentally, the men of Arrah district are very tall. Most of them are strong as well. Having presently been divided into two pieces, the northern part of Shahabad district is called Bhojpur; its headquarters remains in Arrah. The southern part is named Rohatas with its headquarters at Sasaram. Many of you have heard about the strength and bravery of the people of Bhojpur; and the water of Rohatas Districtʼs Bhavuya subdivision is the best [water] in all of Bihar for aiding digestion.

Hence there is no scope for doubting that the people are strong. But for me to jump down from such a height, they had to use all their strength to hold on to the four corners of the dhoti so that those corners would not come out of their hands from the impact of my body. The distortion that comes in the face from employing excessive force was evident in their faces. You must be familiar with this kind of grimace. It is more or less this type of grimace that occurs when one is getting ready to brace for the pain before giving blood or getting an injection. I could see that they were hanging on to the corners of the dhoti with all their might, so I was not worried. At least I knew that if I jumped onto the dhoti, their hands would not slacken and cause me fall to the ground. Just to the side of the men that were holding the dhoti stood several strong young men of twenty-four or twenty-five years of age. They had their hands upraised and were saying: “Donʼt jump onto the dhoti; jump on us instead. We will catch you.”

On one side I was looking at those holding the dhoti and on the other the boys with their upraised hands. Then I asked: “Why is the car over there? What is the harm if I jump onto the hood of the car?” All of them together broke out in a clamour, saying “no, no.” Their contention was that the hood of the car was made of hard metal. I might get hurt if I jumped onto it.

By this time the elephant was almost right up to the wire, hardly ten cubits [4.6 metres] away. A delay of about one more minute and the elephant would run into the wire. A terrible accident would ensue.

I looked at those holding the dhoti, and then I looked at the boys with their upraised arms. Then I looked at the car. Jumping onto the hood of the car would be honorable. Then again, jumping onto the dhoti would be honorable as well. Jumping onto the boys would not be honorable because one or another of the boys could break their hand; someone could also sprain or break a finger. I could see that everyone was ready, waiting for me to jump. The readiness [reflected] on the faces of those holding the dhoti was something to behold. They gave a loud cry: “Jay Bábá, Jay Bábá, Jay Bábá!” I stood up from the throne and climbed up on the silver walls that encircled me. I was then about two stories above the ground. My childhood friend, Shamsu (Shamsujjaman Mallik), who was standing on one side of the elephant, was repeating the name ‘Bismillah’ over and over for my safety. From one edge of the throne, I jumped from the silver wall adorned with bulbs.

But then... what happened then? Did I survive that journey? Yes, I did indeed survive, but there was a little ‘mishap’. It was the end of Áshvin or the beginning of Kárttik, the month of October. For the holidays at that time, I was wearing a brand new, gold-threaded Shantipuri dhoti given to me by my paternal uncle. When I jumped I failed to notice that one corner of my dhoti had become stuck on one of the pointed ends of the throne. So I jumped, but a piece of the dhoti about two cubits long caught on the pointed end and became completely torn up and ruined. Alas, that brand new, gold-threaded, Shantipuri dhoti!

I landed on the hand-held dhoti. The amount of force they exerted was written on their faces. With the shout of “Jay Bábá!” everyone had become anxious. This was their victory as well. I did not fall on the ground. They had caught me. The bhukti pradhán [district secretary] of Arrah was standing just to the side. He rushed over and caught me again, opening the car door and putting me inside, then closing the door behind me. I looked and saw the thrill of victory and sigh of relief on the faces of the boys who had held the dhoti. The boys who had their hands upraised said with regret: “Why didnʼt you jump on us? It would have been fine!”
I looked and saw that the elephant was by then about two cubits away from running into the electric wire. The elephant was still dancing, even though the band had stopped [playing] earlier.

Not only the elephant was dancing, the whole procession was dancing to the beat. The beat was not dying out at all. The beginning of the Bhojpuri song that they were singing is still dancing in my mind.
Tohár carań choŕ Bábá kekar gahab ho,
Kekar gahab ho málik kekar gahab ho.
[Except for your holy feet, whose glory should I sing, O Bábá? Say whose glory I can sing, O my Master.]
The bhukti pradhán said: “It would not be right to keep your car detained in this crowd.”

After seeing me jump off the elephant, the mahout was relieved. Then by beating the elephant repeatedly on the head with his goad, he was able to bring him somewhat under control. He cried out: “Sit Sam, sit Sam, sit Sam.” Harassed and beaten, this time the elephant sat down.
Again the bhukti pradhán said: “It would not be right to keep your car held up in this crowd. Let the procession proceed at its own speed. I will take you on ahead.”

After going ahead a little, I looked behind and saw that the [impending] accident been avoided. The elephant was sitting down, but his trunk was now dancing to the same beat that his feet had been dancing to before. The members of the procession had formed a circle around him, all of them dancing to that same beat. Their joyful sound, their booming “Jay” and the stanzas of their song, were reverberating throughout the atmosphere:
Ánhár bhaila dúr ráh baṋcke calab ho,
Kekar gahab ho málik kekar gahab ho.
[The darkness is gone, behold the proper path and proceed; say O my Master, whose glory can I sing?]
How they danced around the elephant that day! If any of you know the reason for all that commotion, then please tell me. ( 2 )
Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]

According to ancient Puranic legend, on the western bank of the spot where the Náráyańii and Gańd́aka rivers met the Ganges River, a huge elephant and a huge turtle, symbolizing Hari [Lord Krśńa] and Hara [Lord Shiva] respectively, fought a duel. The people came there to organize a big fair annually on the full moon day in the Bengali month of Kárttika [in October during autumn]. Humans, birds and animals dear to Lord Shiva all crowded there together. In order to attract more people, shops were set up for buying and selling food items. People used to gather there in large numbers. Various animals from different parts of the country and abroad, such as elephants, camels, horses, cows, buffaloes, goats and sheep, were brought together at the fair. No other such fair was known to be held anywhere in the world until that time. That fair at the Hari-Hara ground continues to be held even today on the autumnal full moon day.

To the north of the fairground, the rail lines stretch from Hazipur junction to Sonepur junction. Close to the fairground is a huge mango orchard. To the east of the ground is the Náráyańii-Gańd́ak, and beyond it is Vaishali district with Hazipur as the district headquarters. The spot falls under the jurisdiction of Sonepur Police station in Chapra district of Bihar. To the south of this place flows the river Ganges, and the ghat is popularly known as Pahleja Ghat. To the west lies the rest of Chapra district. Although the common language of Chapra district is Bhojpuri, the language of the Sonepur police station area is Bajjiká Maithili.

[As mentioned earlier], for a long time this has been the largest animal fair in the world. Now I am told that in Russia, near Moscow, a similar large animal fair is held. That fair is known to be even larger than the fair on Hazipur fairground nowadays. It is very likely because, with the abolition of the zamindary system, there is hardly any customer for elephants, although there are a few sellers. Few elephants are brought for sale. Is it only because of this? Even if the zamindary system had remained, the import of elephants would still have declined, because elephants are fast being replaced by four-wheeled jeeps. Yet is this the only reason? The elephant consumes every week twenty maunds ( 1 ) of branches, twigs and leaves of trees. During their stay in the forest, an elephant spoils about sixty maunds of such vegetation per week. Every week the elephant has to be provided with eight maunds of rice and half a maund of clarified butter. A mahout has to be employed to tend the elephant. Lest the elephantʼs head turns hot, it has to be regularly bathed in water. The jeep has no such problems. Other than expenses for petrol or diesel and occasional servicing, no other incurring expenditure is involved in its maintenance.

The import of horses has also declined; those who once used them for transport are now using jeeps, motorcycles, scooters, etc. There is now hardly any use for horse-drawn carriages. In its place have come petrol-operated cars and even cars operated by electricity. So the demand for horses and elephants has declined. The use of camels has also decreased, although not by much. As before, the people of northern India use the camel for tilling the soil even today. Whereas for tilling the land one requires at least two bullocks, only one camel will do the same job. And the camel also offers milk. Furthermore, the camel is also the ship of the desert. So the utility of the camel prevails almost as much as before. I say ‘almost’, because for drawing the plough there is increasing use of tractors. Whatever the case might be, the importance of the Hari-Hara fair has noticeably diminished. Yet the glamour of the fair is still there. On account of this animal fair at Hari-Hara grounds, the railway platform of the Sonepur station was once the longest platform in India, probably in the world. Now I learnt that the platform of the Kharagpur station of the South Eastern Railway has wrested that glory. This is quite likely. ( 2 )

In ancient times any secretive slaughter of animals was considered an act of cowardice. Any animal that had less strength than a human being was not directly slaughtered; it was given the opportunity to fight a battle. That was the prevalent system in the pre-Buddhist era. In the Buddhist and post-Buddhist periods, although animal slaughter was not entirely banned, any slaughter of animals on religious grounds was condemned. In a society influenced by the Jain religion, not only for the sake of religion but even for consumption, animal slaughter was considered a lowly and mean act. However, as I was saying, in the pre-Buddhist period, slaughtering an animal secretly was considered a mean act, although people of those days in the name of religion and for the sake of food slaughtered animals and birds.
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: Although they uttered the prayer Sarvaḿ khalvidaḿ Brahma [“Let everyone live in happiness”], yet in the name of religion they committed animal slaughter. They did not oppose the slaughter of innocent animals; in fact, they even supported it. This is quite regrettable. Maybe in those days the mindset of the people was such that the time was not yet ripe for reflecting about animals, birds and plants. Yet there were certain restrictions on animal slaughter. Animal slaughter and meat eating were not permitted on every religious occasion; female animals could not be slaughtered. Domesticated animals could not be slaughtered without giving them the opportunity to give battle. Fish could be caught in a net but could not be caught by using fishing bait or by tempting them with food. Those who did not observe these restrictions were called kut́aka. Forests where animal slaughter was forbidden were known as mrgadáva or sanctuaries (nirbhaya kánan, just as one near Varanasi adjacent to Sarnath was Rśi-pattan Mrgadáva; in the Prákrt language it is called Iśi-pattan Mrgadáva). Those who secretly killed any animal in these protected areas (mrgadávas) were also known as kut́akas. Those who took to this secret killing of animals – their nature was known as kaot́akika. For the word kaot́akika in its etymological sense, one could even use the expression kaot́ika.
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: In common usage, the word kaot́akika would mean “the secret killer of animals”. Those who killed animals without letting anyone know, who disobeyed state injunctions and killed animals secretly (meaning the poachers), those who killed weak animals without giving them the opportunity to defend themselves (that is, the butchers) – all these were known as kaot́akikas.Those who killed animals publicly or secretly, who killed birds and beasts by giving them the opportunity to defend themselves or without giving them any such opportunity, who defied state injunction and killed animals secretively or in secret places, were also called kaotilika (kutilika + ań). They were looked down upon as mean people in the society. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: In ancient times, to please the gods, offerings made by human beings were called grihabali; not only offerings to the gods but even offerings addressed to the forefathers or to please ghosts and spirits were also known as grihabali. Human nature is such that whatever one likes to eat, one believes that others also like to eat the same.
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: One of my distant aunts would invariably offer to a highly placed guest in her house fried cakes of poppy-seeds along with other food items, the reason for which can be easily surmised. Similarly, in those days whatever items people liked to eat, they used to offer them as sacrificial offerings – such as the goat, the buffalo the horse, the heart and liver, and barley. (They came across fine rice and wheat a little later). Not only among the Aryans of those days, but also among people of other religious beliefs in later times, the practice of animal sacrifice persisted. Still later, the whole affair turned into a case of individual liking or preference – whatever they liked, they sacrificed in the name of the gods, ancestors and spirits only nominally, but in reality it was to satisfy their craving to eat those items.
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: Consider a situation where, on the occasion of a religious ceremony, animal sacrifice had still not taken place yet all the arrangements, such as fixing the number of persons to be invited, how many would be offered meat, and so forth, were made beforehand. Verbally it was declared that the animals were being freed from animal life. This [slaughter] of their own dear animals was treated as a sacrifice. We people of common intelligence hardly understand the meaning of this kind of sacrifice. How, by doing harm to someone or putting an end to someoneʼs life, can the [so-called] glory of sacrifice be attained by human beings? It is beyond our common understanding. Is not that sacrifice wherein one gives up something of oneʼs very own the real sacrifice? Is not feasting [with the meat of a sacrificed animal] the rich people or oneʼs own people and hoping to achieve some kind of holiness similar to living in a foolʼs paradise? Is not someone committing these acts at the cost of othersʼ lives?

t: I have heard the story of a man who, after worshipping goddess Káli for fifty years, abruptly ceased. The people of that area asked him, “You there, why have you stopped your worship so suddenly?” He replied sadly, “I have no more teeth.”
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: In the Vedic worship there was the practice of animal sacrifice. The conscience of Vardhaman Mahaviira and Lord Buddha could not accept it. Hence, although accepting the greatness of Buddha in other ways, supporters of the Yajiṋa-cult did not even support his disapproval [of animal sacrifice]. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: Birds and Animals, Our Neighbours [a compilation]
chapterTitle: How Far is Animal Slaughter Justifiable?

t: Growth in the animal population takes place in three ways. First mammals grow in the motherʼs womb in a membrane (placenta), and after attaining their full size they become restless in the womb and are born with the placenta tied to the navel. The nurse severs the link between the navel of the baby and the placenta, which we can describe as analogous to the shell of an egg. Just as the interior of the egg is covered with a shell, the embryo of the mammal similarly remains encased in a placenta. In spoken language this placenta is called phul (in Nepali language the egg is called phul). The life of a child-bearing woman is endangered if the placenta takes a long time to come out of the womb, after the birth of the child. After the placenta comes out of the womb, it is either burnt or buried in the ground [in traditional societies.] For the proper extrication of this placenta, there are certain homeopathic medicines. In ancient Indian therapeutics, certain instruments were recommended or used for extricating the dead baby from the womb, for bringing out the placenta, or for bringing out the live baby from the womb; they were called garbhashauṋku.

These mammals have to depend on the motherʼs milk after their birth. If the baby continues to be fed wholly on the motherʼs milk, without being given any other food for quite some time, it will still be hale and hearty, just like the children of cows, buffaloes and other animals. That which comes out of the motherʼs body as milk essence, which is a metamorphosed form of motherʼs blood, is termed as stan – root verb + yat suffix = stanna. Stan + ac = Stan [breast] means “the motherʼs milk which provides essential calcium for the nutritional well-being of the baby”. Be it formula milk, milk from the midwife, powdered milk, or the milk of the female donkey – none is comparable to the motherʼs milk. So, those who deprive the baby of motherʼs milk do maximum harm to the baby. How much humans or animals are indebted to their mother becomes evident from the fact that right from the earliest stage in the womb, the blood and vitality of the baby comes from the motherʼs body. Even after birth, for quite some time the baby is nourished from motherʼs milk which was transmuted from the motherʼs blood. So in ancient India, probably for this reason, the father is compared to heaven by saying:
Pitá svarga pitá dharma, pitáhi paramantapah
Pitari priitimápanne priiyante sarva devatáh.
[The father is heaven, the father is dharma, the father is supremely adorable; if the father is pleased, all the gods are pleased.]
But the mother is coupled with the motherland; it is said:
Jananii janmabhumisca svargádapi gariiyasii.
That is, the mother is something even superior to heaven. That is why Tantra has asked all people to treat every woman as akin to mother.

The transformation from oviparous creatures to mammals has led to significant complexities in the animal body. In some countries of the world there are animals which are midway between the oviparous and the mammal stage. The (duckbill) platypus is such a creature. Closely related to the cat; the duckbill (platypus) lays eggs, yet it is a mammal. Bats are much closer to mammals than the duckbill (platypus). They give birth to young ones, which remain in an immature state after birth. Akin to the bat order – perhaps its sub-order – is the vampire [bird; Geospiza nebulosa or sharp-beaked finch] and the titmouse (cámciká). These two belong to the same order. Whether they are oviparous or mammalian, the progeny of all creatures remain helpless after birth for some time. The home for these helpless babies is the “lying-in-room” or “birthing room”. The newborn child is entirely helpless – frail and helpless (árta or átura). That is why the birthing room is called the room for the helpless; in colloquial Bengali it is called áturghar (áturálaya) or “sick-room”.

After the baby is born, so long as its ten different sense organs do not work properly, it is treated as if it were still in the womb or garbha. The human baby is assisted by the nurse to enable its sense organs to function. When she inserts something in the mouth, the baby expels the accumulated saliva and then, stimulated by this action, cries out. If the baby does not cry, it should be understood that it has little chance of survival. So, the mild sound of the first cry of the human or animal baby is the very sign of life.
Tulsi jab tum jag men áyo jag haṋse tum roye,
Aesii karńii karke calo háṋso tum jag roye.
[Tulsi, when you came into this world, it smiled and you wept. Continue your noble deeds so that when you die, you will smile and the world will weep.]

So long as the baby does not cry, declaring its existence, it is considered to be still in the motherʼs womb. When the nurse extricates the accumulated saliva from the babyʼs mouth, in rural Bengal this is called “making a start with the mouth”. When an adolescent speaks impudently in the presence of elders, the elderly person might say, “Listen, listen to his impudent words. Even now he has not made a start with his mouth, listen to the hollowness of his words!”

When the foetus in the motherʼs womb becomes somewhat developed, its hair starts to grow. The mother may develop nausea. Sometimes she develops a special fascination with certain edibles and inedibles, and some peculiar distastes as well. In ancient Bengal there was a social custom to provide an opportunity to a pregnant woman to eat foods of her choice. This was known as sádhbhakśań.

Normally, in the advanced stage of pregnancy, women are not permitted to do physical labour. This is wrong. Women in that condition should be allowed to do a little work. (The same principle applies to pregnant animals.) Otherwise, there remains a risk during labour. Pregnant women and female animals may work half of what they usually do at other times; but under no circumstances should they be allowed to do strenuous work, as it may lead to premature delivery or stillbirth.

Foods which are highly acidic, such as acidic citrus fruits, overripe pineapples, overripe jám, cottonseed flour and spicy pickles, should be carefully avoided as they may harm the fetus. Bending over in a stooping posture to lift anything heavy is strictly forbidden for pregnant women. Although there is no objection to carrying loads for those who are accustomed to it, they must not stoop over to lift a heavy load onto their heads. It is better if others will help them to lift it up. In this stage of pregnancy a daily bath is a rule, but one must not bathe after sunset. It is better to lie down on a hard bed.

It is desirable that the best room in the house should be used for the confinement. In certain parts of rural Bengal, the worst room or the cowshed is used for confinement out of superstition. This practice is certainly wrong – more than that, it is a crime.

There are many people who affect respect, loudly praising women as a race of mothers, but who in practical life suppress them underfoot, sending them into the jaws of premature death by depriving them of happiness and the comforts of life. The conscientious should be vocal against these heinous acts. We must pay due honour to women as mothers and help them to live long lives.

The family should see to it that the woman is not forced to walk to the outhouse on foot for at least twenty-four hours after delivery. The delivery room should be fitted with a bathtub and commode. If a girl is born no one in the family is to point an accusing finger, either directly or indirectly, at the mother. It may create undue pressure on her heart. There was one lady of my acquaintance who was unable to bear the humiliation brought down by her family just after the birth of her seventh daughter. She cried out, “Again a daughter, again a daughter, again a daughter!” and immediately expired.

A pregnant woman must certainly be provided with nutritious food. No constipation-creating foods should be supplied to her. This is as applicable to animal mothers as to human mothers. Sweet-pea leaves, or if not available, then spinach, nat́e shák or gourd leaves should be taken daily in small amounts. Puṋi shák should be strictly avoided.

All that I have said in the above is as applicable to pregnant animals as it is to human mothers. In the case of the first delivery one should consult a physician or experienced midwife after one month. If one follows the above instructions, death during delivery will become a rare phenomenon.

Some people cultivate their land using cows, and others even use them to draw carts. I do not know what other tasks are performed with the help of cows, but I would dissuade people from compelling pregnant cows to till their soil, draw their carts and run their oil mills. This is an inhuman act and is contradictory to principles of Neo-humanism.

For cows whose pregnancy is very advanced, green grass is indispensable. If at that stage the cows are not able to graze in the field, their caretaker must bring cut grass to give them. Whether it helps that caretaker to reach heaven is immaterial; but it is sure to lay the foundation of Neo-humanism:
Gokál gokule bás
Gabeer mukhe diye ghás
Ámár habe svargavás.
[The cow lives at Gokula,
Making the grass available to the cow,
I will surely go to heaven.]
Whether the person goes to heaven or not, at least they will be performing a great duty. ( 1 )

The subject of todayʼs discourse is, “Renaissance in all the strata of life.”
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: The real meaning of the word “renaissance” is reawakening. That is, humanity was sleeping, and now it must wake up from the cimmerian slumber and do something in all the spheres of life, in all the strata of existence.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: There are three important strata in life: the physical stratum, the psychic stratum and the spiritual stratum. In the physical stratum, there are many strata: say, scientific achievement, social progress, political life, economic life, culture life. People often say that this twentieth century is the century of science. No, it is not the truth. Human life has been associated with science from the prehistoric era, from the very birth of humanity on this earth about one million years ago, and not only in this twentieth century. And as long as there will be a single human being, there will be an age of science.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: Nowadays science means creating new weapons – strengthening the hands of warmongers; but the spirit of science should not be like this, and at the start, in the primordial phase of human life, it was not so. Yes, there is necessity of weapons – weapons not for strengthening the hands of warmongers, but for providing security for good ideas, good thoughts and good persons.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: Science should be just like art: science for service and beatitude. Art for service and beatitude, I said; and now I say, science is also for service and beatitude. Science should always be utilized for the proper progress of human society.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: Then the social. In the social sphere there are several sub-strata, and the real spirit of social progress is to dispel all social disparities. Each and every member of the human society should enjoy equal rights as members of the same family, but there is disparity and it is the duty of the Renaissance movement to dispel the disparity and bring about equality, equilibrium and equipoise amongst human beings.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: There are disparities, disparities of different types and different kinds. For instance, there are biological disparities existing in the society, which are being encouraged by certain selfish persons. The biological disparity between human and animal, between human and plant, between animal and plant – that disparity must not be there. Just as a human being wants to survive, a pigeon also wants to survive – similarly a cow also wants to survive, or a tree. Just as my life is dear to me, so the lives of created beings are also equally dear to them. It is the birthright of human beings to live in this world, and it is the birthright of the animal world and plant world also to remain on this earth. To recognize this right, and to get it recognized by the entire human society, the Renaissance movement will have to do something concrete.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: Then there are physico-psychic ailments. Some people argue that animals have been created by Parama Puruśa for our food. I knew a certain person who used to say that if people do not eat goatsʼ meat, the world would become populated only by goats. And others said that if people do not eat chickens, there would not be even a single inch of space on this earth – it would be filled with chickens! Now my point is, even though human beings do not eat vultures, is there a crowd of vultures in the world? How foolish such people are! People do not eat earthworms – has there been an uncontrollable growth of earthworms on earth? Only out of excessive greed, people eat chickens and goats and are simply searching for logic to support their actions and cover up their weakness. This sort of cunning will not do. In the mobility of the psychic world, there are certain defective thoughts prevailing – that we humans are destined to rule this earth, and the creatures are destined to be ruled by us. You will have to fight against this type of psychology with the help of your strong weapon. What is that weapon? Neohumanism. All have the equal right to live here: this universe is for all. It is not the patrimony of human beings only. This is also the duty of renaissance people. ( 1 )

chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: As human beings progress towards the realm of spirituality, they are helped on the one hand by PROUT, which guarantees minimum requirements and maximum amenities, and on the other hand by Neohumanistic outlook, which removes disparities. These two approaches help human beings in their progress and elevation. Finally the existential faculty merges in the Supreme.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: Neohumanism also touches the threshold point of spirituality. It helps the existential faculty reach the pinnacled state. Neohumanism will bring equality in the social sphere and remove all sorts of disparities, therefore human progress will be greatly accelerated.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: When PROUT and Neohumanism are established, the whole existence of human beings will become effulgent in the attainment of the Supreme.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: At present human beings are thinking about their own minimum requirements more than about the minimum requirements of animals and plants. A day is coming when some of the animals, if not all, will come within the realm of our social membership. Today we say that each and every human being will get the minimum requirements. Tomorrow we will say that the minimum requirements will also include the needs of dogs, cows, monkeys, etc. To fulfil these requirements, there should be more and more production.
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: The earth is not only for human beings, it is for other living beings also. So we will have to do something for them. The minimum requirements and maximum amenities should also be given to animals. Today cows, dogs and monkeys are developing; tomorrow more and more animals will be in this category. Animals will also develop longings for different psycho-physical pabula, so they should be guaranteed minimum requirements and maximum amenities too. We will have to do something for them also. This is the demand of Neohumanism, of Neo-Humanistic ideas. This demand should be fulfilled by PROUT. ( 2 )

t: Charter of Rights
chapterTitle: Renaissance in All the Strata / Economic and Constitutional Guarantees for Animalsʼ Rights

t: The formation of a World Government will require a world constitution. A charter of principles or bill of rights should be included in such a constitution and encompass at least the following four areas. First, complete security should be guaranteed to all the plants and animals on the planet. Secondly, each country must guarantee purchasing power to all its citizens. Thirdly, the constitution should guarantee four fundamental rights – spiritual practice or Dharma; cultural legacy; education; and indigenous linguistic expression. Fourthly, if the practice of any of these rights conflicts with cardinal human values then that practice should be immediately curtailed. That is, cardinal human values must take precedence over all other rights. All the constitutions of the world suffer from numerous defects. The above points may be adopted by the framers of different constitutions to overcome these defects. ( 3 )

t: Yacchedváuṋmanasiiprájiṋastadyacchejjiṋána átmani;
Jiṋánamátmani mahati niyacchettadyacchecchánta átmani.

[Wise persons first merge their indriyas [sense organs] into their citta [mind-stuff], then their citta into aham [doer-I], then aham into mahat [“I exist” feeling], then mahat into jiivátmá [unit spirit, soul], and finally their jiivátmá into Paramátmá, Supreme Consciousness.]

I have already told you how spiritual aspirants should live their lives. I have said that a real sadhaka [spiritual aspirant] will properly discharge their duties in the relative world, and will at the same time attend properly to their duties in the spiritual world; and between the two worlds, there will be a happy blending. In the external world there should be an objective adjustment, and at the same time there should, in the psychic world, be a subjective approach.

Furthermore, never forgetting that human life is an ideological flow, human beings should always move towards the supreme ideology. They have been moving in this direction since time immemorial and, through this process of movement, have reached the present stage of humanity. Passing through many lives as worms, insects, birds, and animals, they have undergone countless pains, miseries, tortures and humiliations. Take for example the life of a goat. A goat spends its life eating grass, until the day comes when the butcher grabs it, kills it, skins it and sells its flesh piece by piece in the market. That goat at one time had to live such a miserable life. But today it has forgotten all this. Through a process of forward movement, today it may have attained a human life.

Human life is more secure than animal life. Many animals live in the jungle where there is something to fear every minute; where the weak are the prey of the strong. To escape this atmosphere of fear and insecurity, many wild animals have sought refuge with human beings. They have been fed grass, leaves and other types of fodder until the right moment came to kill them for their flesh. Even today, this is generally what happens. Animals fully trust human beings; they trust them even up to one minute before their death. But when they see a person approaching them with a weapon in hand, they realize that those they had trusted as their friends are actually their enemies. Although human beings feed their animals, the love or attachment which they have for them is purely external. There is no genuine love in [humans]. This is how wretched animal life can be.

Every human being has had to pass through that sort of painful animal life in the past. But that does not mean we should be the cause of misery for those animals who have taken shelter with us today. On the contrary, we should have a merciful attitude towards them. A woman who has been badly treated or humiliated by her mother-in-law should be careful that she does not treat her daughter-in-law in the same way. Human beings should carry out their duties properly in the external world and should always ensure that no being suffers unnecessarily from any undue mistreatment. In the physical sphere, the rights of all should be protected. Each and every human being should be guaranteed the basic necessities of life: food, clothing, medicine, shelter and education. “I wonʼt exploit anyone, and I will not allow others to exploit me.” This is the spirit of proper objective adjustment. And while this proper objective adjustment is maintained, work must continue in a progressive way. You will have to move ahead on the path of life while keeping an adjustment with the external world.

You must always remember that your existence is not only a physical one. It is animals who are primarily concerned with the physical world, who struggle merely to survive. Those animals which live in jungles are constantly confronted by the fear of tigers, lions, bears, elephants, snakes, crocodiles and a host of other ferocious creatures; while those which have surrendered to human beings, such as goats, sheep and cows, are confronted in the last moment of their lives with the fear of being slaughtered by a human. So it is quite obvious that animal life is less secure than human life.

In todayʼs world, human beings face difficulties in maintaining an objective adjustment with the physical world. As we have not yet been able to build an ideal human society, we will have to first concentrate on providing everyone with the basic requirements of life. Once that task is accomplished, we will be able to build an ideal society. To enable society to progress spiritually, people will be given sufficient scope and time for spiritual practices.

The subjective approach is to first withdraw the crude mind gradually from the external world and merge it in the subtle mind, and then to merge the subtle mind in unit consciousness. When unit consciousness is merged in Cosmic Consciousness, a human being is said to have attained the supreme fulfilment in life. In the present world, human beings face such tremendous difficulties in maintaining their objective adjustment that they cannot afford to give any time for their subjective approach. This is the greatest tragedy of the day! That is why I would like to advise you to build a healthy human society as early as possible, so that each and every human being gets enough scope and time for spiritual progress. ( 1 )

Neohumanism in a Nutshell Part 1 [a compilation]
ÁJIṊÁ CAKRA: Sixth, or lunar, psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus; the “yogic wisdom eye”. See also CAKRA.
ANÁHATA CAKRA: Fourth psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus; the “yogic heart”. See also CAKRA.
ÁNANDA: Divine bliss.
ANANDA MARGA: Path of divine bliss; Ánanda Márga Pracáraka Saḿgha (Ananda Marga organization).

ANANDANAGAR: Situated in the hilly terrain of Purulia District (West Bengal), in the midst of beautiful natural surroundings, this is the registered headquarters of Ananda Marga where multifarious welfare activities such as education, relief, ecological preservation, integrated village development, etc., are conducted. Many old Tantra piit́has (spiritual meditation sites) are situated here.
ANGIKA, AUṊGIKÁ: A language of the eastern demi-Mágadhii group (Bengali, Oriya, etc.) spoken in Bhagalpur, Purnia, and some other areas of Bihar.
ÁTMÁ, ÁTMAN: Soul, consciousness, Puruśa, pure cognition. The átman of the Cosmos is PARAMÁTMAN, and that of the unit is the jiivátman.
BÁBÁ: Literally, “dear” or “dearest One”. It may be used to refer to PARAMA PURUŚA, and is an affectionate name for Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti.

BHÁGAVATA DHARMA: The “divine” DHARMA of human beings, i.e., the dharma to attain the Supreme. Bhágavata dharma rests on four pillars: 1) vistára (expansion); 2) rasa (literally “flow” – surrender); 3) sevá (service); 4) tadsthiti (final ensconcement in the Supreme).
BRAHMA: Supreme Entity, comprising both Puruśa, or SHIVA, and Prakrti, or Shakti
BUDDHA: One who has attained bodhi, intuition. Lord Buddha, the propounder of Buddhism, appeared approximately 2500 years ago.

CAKRA: Cycle or circle; psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus. The cakras in the human body are all located along the suśumná canal which passes through the length of the spinal column and extends up to the crown of the head. Some cakras, however, are associated with external concentration points. The concentration points: (1) for the múládhára cakra, the base of the spine, above the perineum; (2) for the svádhiśt́hána, the genital organ; (3) for the mańipura, the navel; (4) for the anáhata, the midpoint of the chest; (5) for the vishuddha, the throat; (6) for the ájiṋá, between the eyebrows; and (7) for the sahasrára, the crown of the head. There are two other cakras which are needed in certain spiritual practices, so the cakras are nine in number.
DHARMA: Characteristic property; spirituality; the path of righteousness in social affairs.
GAŃESHA: In mythology, the son of Shiva; god of commerce; half man, half elephant.
GURU: Gu means “darkness”, ru means “dispeller”; hence “dispeller of darkness”; spiritual master.

HARA: Literally, “the entity which is instrumental for the withdrawal of everything” (the word is derived from ha and ra – ha is the acoustic root of the ethereal factor and ra is the acoustic root of energy) or “one who undergoes no change under the influence of others”; other names of Lord Shiva.

HARI: Literally, “that which steals”; one who steals othersʼ sins to lighten their burden and pave the way for their liberation; another name of Parama Puruśa – the entity responsible for the preservation of unit beings.
KÁLII: Goddess Kálii; one of the three consorts of Sadáshiva, an Austrico-Dravidian girl.
KAORAVAS: Hundred sons of King Dhritarastra, the adhármika forces in the Mahábhárata war.
KAOŚIKI/KAOSHIKII SATTÁ: Prakrti, the Operative Principle, in the first stage of creation, before the development of the imbalance in the triangle of forces. The energy of Prakrti.
KIIRTANA: Collective singing of the name of the Lord, combined with instrumental music and with a dance that expresses the spirit of surrender.

KRŚŃA, SHRII KRŚŃA: Literally, “the entity which attracts everything of the universe towards its own self”, PARAMA PURUŚA. A great Tantric guru, the historical Krśńa of about 1500 BC; second advent of TÁRAKA BRAHMA (an advent is known as Mahásambhúti).
KURUKŚETRA: Literally, a field always saying “Kuru, kuru,” “Do something, do something;” hence the world, the entire universe; the place where the Mahábhárata war was fought; a town near Delhi.
MAGAHII: A language of the western demi-Mágadhii group (Bhojpuri, Chattisgarhii, etc.) spoken in Patna, Gaya, Aurangabad, Daltonganj and some other areas of Bihar.
MAHÁBHÁRATA: “Great India”; the name of a military campaign guided by Lord Krśńa around 1500 BCE to unify India; the epic poem written by Maharshi Vyasa about this campaign.
MAHÁYÁNII/MAHÁYÁNA: One of the two major schools of Buddhism, the northern school as opposed to the southern school, or Hiinayána Buddhism.
MANTRA: A sound or collection of sounds which, when meditated upon, will lead to spiritual liberation. A mantra is incantative, pulsative and ideative.
NÁRÁYAŃA: The Supreme Entity; literally, “the Lord of Nára (Prakrti)”.
OTA YOGA: The association of Puruśottama with each unit creation individually in His introversial movement; Puruśottamaʼs intimate relation with every entity.
PANDAVAS: The five sons of King Pandu, representing the dhármika forces in the Mahábhárata war.
PARAMA PURUŚA: Supreme Consciousness.
PARAMÁTMÁ, PARAMÁTMAN: Supreme Consciousness as the witness of His own Macropsychic conation.
PÁRVATII: The colloquial version of “Parvata Kanyá” – “Daughter of the Mountains”; one of the three wives of Sadáshiva.
PRÁKRTA: The seven spoken languages that developed from Sanskrit; prákrta also means prákrta janas, that is, “common people”.
PROTA YOGA: The association of Puruśottama with all creation in His extroversial movement and with all the unit creations collectively in His extroversial movement.
PURANA: Mythological story with a moral impact; educative fiction.
RÁMÁYAŃA: An epic poem of India. It is the story of King Rama, or Ramchandra.
RAŔH: The territory, mostly in modern-day Bengal and Jharkhand, stretching from the west bank of the Bhagirathi River to the Parasnath Hills.
SÁDHANÁ: Literally, “ sustained effort”; spiritual practice; meditation.
SAHASRÁRA CAKRA: Highest, or pineal, psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus, located at the crown of the head. See also CAKRA.
SAḾSKÁRA: Mental reactive momentum, potential mental reaction.

SANSKRIT, SAḾSKRTA: The classical language of India. It first emerged during the Post-Shiva period, and as a spoken language it began to be supplanted by Prákrta prior to the Krśńa period. Although not a spoken language today except in very limited circumstances, it is still important for its vast literature, especially spiritual literature. Sanskrit and English are the languages of the world that have the richest vocabularies. Sanskrit pronunciation was perfected by non-Aryan Tantrics in such a way that each of the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet constitutes one acoustic root of Tantra.

SHIVA: A great Tantric guru of 5000 BCE who guided society while His mind was absorbed in Consciousness; hence, Infinite Consciousness, Puruśa. First advent of TÁRAKA BRAHMA (an advent is known as Mahásambhúti).
SHLOKA: A Sanskrit couplet expressing one idea.
SITA: Wife of Rama.

TANTRA: A spiritual tradition which originated in India in prehistoric times and was first systematized by Shiva. It emphasizes the development of human vigour, both through meditation and through confrontation of difficult external situations, to overcome all fears and weakness. Also, a scripture expounding that tradition.
TÁRAKA BRAHMA: Supreme Consciousness in Its liberating aspect.

VEDA: Literally, “knowledge”; hence, a composition imparting spiritual knowledge. Also, a religious or philosophical school which originated among the Aryans and was brought by them to India. It is based on the Vedas and emphasizes the use of ritual to gain the intervention of the gods.
VISHUDDHA CAKRA: Fifth psycho-spiritual centre, or plexus, related to the vocal cord and to the thyroid and parathyroid glands; controls sixteen propensities. See also CAKRA.
VIŚŃU: Literally, “entity which pervades each and every thing”; All-Pervading Entity; Preserving Entity; a mythological god.
VRTTI: Mental propensity.
YOGA: Spiritual practice leading to unification of the unit átman with Paramátman.
